4.2.常见读法: Poverty can corrupt people and so can wealth; judge people over the long run.
4.2.字眼: “乐”音洛 — le read luo; “约，穷困也” — yue means poverty and hardship; “利，犹贪也，盖深知笃好而必欲得之也” — li means craving: knowing it deeply, loving it earnestly, and determined to have it; “不仁之人，失其本心，久约必滥，久乐必淫” — the inhumane have lost their original heart: long in hardship they run wild, long in pleasure they overindulge; “惟仁者则安其仁而无适不然，知者则利于仁而不易所守……皆非外物所能夺矣” — the humane rest in humaneness wherever they are, and the wise benefit from it and do not change what they hold to; nothing outside can take it from them.
4.2.诸家: Xie Liangzuo: “仁者心无内外远近精粗之间，非有所存而自不亡，非有所理而自不乱，如目视而耳听，手持而足行也” — for the humane there is no gap of inner and outer, near and far, coarse and fine; nothing is held yet nothing is lost, nothing is arranged yet nothing is disordered, like eyes seeing, ears hearing, hands holding and feet walking; “安仁则一，利仁则二” — resting in humaneness is one, profiting from it is two (the passage “知者谓之有所见则可……未能无意也” in between is left out of the video).
4.2.片里落点: Long hardship makes people overstep, long pleasure makes them indulge; whether outside things can take a person away depends on whether the original heart is there. Today: someone out of work for six months still gets up at seven, shaves, and goes out for a run.

zb_say.yang: The inhumane cannot long endure poverty or ease; the humane rest in ren, the wise profit by ren. Zhu explains by the original heart and firm love; Yang's translation explains 利 by ren's effects.
zb_say.qian: Both gloss 约 as hardship; resting in ren is natural, profiting by ren is knowing ren is good and wanting it. Neither reads it as using ren for outside gain; Qian further speaks of a settled state of mind.

4.3.title: Only the humane can love and hate others
4.3.yw: The Master said: Only the humane can love others and can hate others.
4.3.常见读法: The humane have strong likes and dislikes (with the stress on “daring to hate”).
4.3.字眼: hao (love) and wu (hate) in the departing tone; “唯之为言独也” — “only” means alone; “盖无私心，然后好恶当于理，程子所谓得其公正是也” — only without selfish attachment do likes and dislikes accord with principle — what Cheng Yi called being impartial and right.
4.3.诸家: You Zuo: “好善而恶恶，天下之同情，然人每失其正者，心有所系而不能自克也。惟仁者无私心，所以能好恶也” — loving good and hating bad is common to everyone, yet people often lose rightness because the heart is tied to something and cannot master itself; only the humane, free of selfishness, can truly love and hate.
4.3.片里落点: Everyone can like and dislike; the “can” lies in doing it rightly, which requires a heart that is not tied to anything. Today: a competition judge who sees a former student take the stage stands up, leaves the panel and gives no score for that round.

zb_say.yang: The humane love and hate fittingly; Yang cites “getting the mean”, Zhu explains by having no selfishness and being fair; it does not mean the humane only love and never dislike.
zb_say.qian: Both: without selfish desire, love and hate are right. Qian unfolds how selfish desire keeps love and hate from being true and its social effect; Zhu sums it as a heart without selfishness, loving and hating as principle requires, fair.

4.4.title: Set your heart on humaneness and there is no evil
4.4.yw: The Master said: If one truly sets one's heart on humaneness, there will be no evil.
4.4.常见读法: Once you have made up your mind, you will never make mistakes.
4.4.字眼: e (evil) read in its usual tone; “苟，诚也” — gou means truly; “志者，心之所之也” — will is where the heart goes; “其心诚在于仁，则必无为恶之事矣” — if the heart is truly set on humaneness, there will certainly be no evil deeds.
4.4.诸家: Yang Shi: “苟志于仁，未必无过举也，然而为恶则无矣” — setting one's heart on humaneness does not mean never erring, but there will be no doing of evil.
4.4.片里落点: Resolve does not guarantee no mistakes; it guarantees no intention to do wrong. Today: a learner driver scrapes the car three times in a year but never once runs a red light.

zb_say.yang: One truly set on ren will not do evil; Zhu separates a slip from doing evil, and Yang's translation does not equate an occasional fault with lacking resolve for ren.
zb_say.qian: Qian mainly reads 恶 as wù, hating: one set on ren dislikes people yet still from love; Zhu reads 恶 as è, evil: truly set on ren, one does no evil. Qian also keeps the latter reading.

3.24.title: The border warden of Yi asks to see him
3.24.yw: The border warden of Yi asked to be presented, saying: Whenever a gentleman comes here, I have never failed to see him. The followers presented him. Coming out, he said: My friends, why worry about his losing office? The world has long been without the Way; Heaven is going to use your master as a wooden-tongued bell.
3.24.常见读法: Losing office turned out to be a good thing?
3.24.字眼: xian (be presented) read xian, sang (lose) in the departing tone; “仪，卫邑。封人，掌封疆之官，盖贤而隐于下位者也” — Yi was a town of Wei; the border warden kept the frontier, probably a worthy man hidden in a low post; “木铎，金口木舌，施政教时所振，以警众者也” — the muduo is a bell with a metal mouth and wooden clapper, shaken when proclaiming government and teaching, to alert the crowd; “封人一见夫子而遽以是称之，其所得于观感之间者深矣” — that the warden, on seeing the Master once, at once called him this shows how deeply he perceived him.
3.24.诸家: Zhu Xi records two readings side by side: ① “乱极当治，天必将使夫子得位设教，不久失位也” — disorder at its height must turn to order; Heaven will surely give the Master a post to teach, and he will not be out of office long; ② another view, “天使夫子失位，周流四方以行其教，如木铎之徇于道路也” — Heaven made the Master lose office so he would travel the four quarters spreading his teaching, as the bell is carried along the roads. Zhu Xi does not choose for the reader.
3.24.片里落点: A minor official saw Confucius's weight at first sight. Today: an old teacher moved off the podium runs free classes in the community, and more people come than were ever in his class.

zb_say.yang: 丧 in the departing tone: losing office; the wooden clapper stands for teaching from office, Yang renders it “teacher of the people”. Zhu also keeps the reading of wandering and teaching after losing office, so Zhu does not have only one reading.
zb_say.qian: Qian: having lost office, he wanders to spread the Way; Zhu first: he will gain office and teach, then also lists teaching while out of office. Qian's choice is the same as Zhu's second reading.

3.25.title: The Shao is perfectly beautiful and perfectly good
3.25.yw: The Master said of the Shao: Perfectly beautiful, and perfectly good. He said of the Wu: Perfectly beautiful, but not perfectly good.
3.25.常见读法: Equally beautiful — so where is the difference?
3.25.字眼: “韶，舜乐。武，武王乐。美者，声容之盛。善者，美之实也” — the Shao is Shun's music, the Wu King Wu's; beauty is the fullness of sound and dance, goodness is the substance of beauty; “其功一也，故其乐皆尽美” — their achievements were the same, so both musics are perfectly beautiful; “舜之德，性之也，又以揖逊而有天下；武王之德，反之也，又以征诛而得天下，故其实有不同者” — Shun's virtue was by nature, and he gained the world by yielding; King Wu's virtue was regained, and he won the world by conquest, so in substance they differ.
3.25.诸家: Cheng Yi: “成汤放桀，惟有惭德，武王亦然，故未尽善” — when Tang banished Jie he felt ashamed, and so did King Wu, hence “not perfectly good”; “尧舜汤武，其揆一也。征伐非其所欲，所遇之时然尔” — Yao, Shun, Tang and Wu were one in principle; conquest was not what they wanted, only what their times demanded.
3.25.片里落点: The difference is in how it came: one was yielded, one was taken by force. Today: two equally splendid wins, one earned head-on, one after the opponent withdrew injured — the podium does not taste the same.

zb_say.yang: Shao is wholly beautiful and wholly good, Wu wholly beautiful but not wholly good, tied to abdication and conquest; Yang separates beauty and goodness by sound and content, Zhu by sound and spectacle versus substance.
zb_say.qian: Both: beauty is sound and spectacle, goodness the inner meaning; Shun abdicated, King Wu conquered, hence the difference in goodness. Zhu also explains levels of virtue by “by nature” and “by return”; Qian does not divide them that way.

3.26.title: High position without generosity
3.26.yw: The Master said: Holding high position without generosity, performing ritual without reverence, attending mourning without grief — how could I bear to look at it?
3.26.字眼: sang (mourning) in the level tone; “居上主于爱人，故以宽为本。为礼以敬为本。临丧以哀为本” — holding high position is about loving people, so generosity is its root; reverence is the root of ritual; grief is the root of mourning; “既无其本，则以何者而观其所行之得失哉” — without the root, by what could one judge the rights and wrongs of what they do?
3.26.片里落点: It is not that it looks bad; there is nothing left to look at. Today: the man on the phone talking business at the door of the funeral hall — however large his gift, no one remembers he came.

zb_say.yang: Generosity in high office, reverence in ritual, grief at mourning are the root; Zhu: without the root there is nothing to judge conduct by; Yang renders it freely as “I cannot bear to watch”.
zb_say.qian: Both: generosity is the root of high office, reverence of ritual, grief of mourning; without the root one cannot assess conduct. Qian also takes 临丧 as being in mourning, not only attending a condolence.

4.5.title: Wealth and rank are what people want
4.5.yw: The Master said: Wealth and rank are what people want; if not obtained by the proper way, one does not keep them. Poverty and lowliness are what people hate; if not come by through the proper way, one does not escape them. If a gentleman leaves humaneness, how can he make a name? A gentleman does not depart from humaneness even for the space of a meal; in haste he holds to it, in upheaval he holds to it.
4.5.常见读法: “Not by the proper way” read the same both times — then why not escape a poverty one did not deserve?
4.5.字眼: wu (hate) in the departing tone; “不以其道得之，谓不当得而得之” — “not by the proper way” means getting what one should not get; “于富贵则不处，于贫贱则不去，君子之审富贵而安贫贱也如此” — he does not keep such wealth and does not dodge such poverty: this is how a gentleman weighs wealth and rests in poverty; wu (how) read wu; “若贪富贵而厌贫贱，则是自离其仁，而无君子之实矣” — to crave wealth and loathe poverty is to leave one's own humaneness, with nothing of the gentleman left; “终食者，一饭之顷。造次，急遽苟且之时。颠沛，倾覆流离之际” — a meal is the time of one meal; zaoci is a moment of haste; dianpei is a time of upheaval and displacement.
4.5.诸家: Zhu Xi at the end of the chapter: “取舍之分明，然后存养之功密；存养之功密，则其取舍之分益明矣” — when the line between taking and refusing is clear, the work of preserving and nurturing becomes close; when that work is close, the line becomes clearer still.
4.5.片里落点: Do not take wealth that should not come, and do not dodge an undeserved poverty by crooked means; the big choices and the small daily work make each other. Today: the bus brakes hard, and the young man's first grab is to steady the old woman beside him.

zb_say.yang: Yang thinks the second 得 should be 去 and translates by the chapter's spirit: not escaping poverty by improper means; Zhu keeps 得, meaning getting what one should not get, never leaving ren in poverty or success.
zb_say.qian: Qian reads 得之 with what follows, Zhu reads 不以其道得之 together; both explain by getting what one should not, not keeping such wealth, not dodging such poverty: ren does not shift with circumstances.

4.6.title: I have not seen one who loves humaneness
4.6.yw: The Master said: I have not seen one who loves humaneness or one who hates what is not humane. One who loves humaneness puts nothing above it; one who hates what is not humane practises humaneness by not letting the inhumane touch his person. Is there anyone who can spend his strength on humaneness for a single day? I have not seen one whose strength was not enough. Perhaps there are such, but I have not seen them.
4.6.常见读法: Failing at it is a matter of ability?
4.6.字眼: hao (love) and wu (hate) in the departing tone; “好仁者真知仁之可好，故天下之物无以加之” — one who loves humaneness truly knows it is lovable, so nothing in the world can be put above it; “恶不仁者……必能绝去不仁之事，而不使少有及于其身” — one who hates the inhumane can cut it off entirely and not let the least of it reach him; “此皆成德之事，故难得而见之也” — both are matters of perfected virtue, hence rarely seen; “为仁在己，欲之则是，而志之所至，气必至焉” — humaneness lies with oneself: want it and it is there; where the will goes, the strength follows; “盖，疑辞。有之，谓有用力而力不足者” — gai expresses doubt; “there are such” means people who try but whose strength fails.
4.6.诸家: Zhu Xi on “perhaps there are such”: “人之气质不同，故疑亦容或有此昏弱之甚……盖不敢终以为易，而又叹人之莫肯用力于仁也” — people differ in endowment, so perhaps a few are that dull and weak; he would not call it easy after all, and also sighs that people will not spend their strength on humaneness.
4.6.片里落点: Where the heart goes, the strength goes; the hard part is not strength but willingness. Today: the person with no time to exercise scrolls the phone for two hours before bed.

zb_say.yang: Loving ren puts nothing above it; hating the inhumane keeps it off oneself. For 盖 Yang renders “probably there are those whose strength is not enough”; Zhu too doubts there are but has not seen them; it must not be read as saying everyone has already tried their best.
zb_say.qian: Qian disagrees with splitting loving ren and hating the inhumane into two grades of person, stressing one and the same heart of love and hate; Zhu speaks of two kinds of perfected virtue. The reading that nothing in the world can be put above ren is close.

4.7.title: People's faults each follow their kind
4.7.yw: The Master said: People's faults each belong to their kind. Look at the fault, and you will know the humaneness.
4.7.常见读法: So one fault is enough to judge a person?
4.7.字眼: “党，类也” — dang means kind, type; Zhu Xi's own note: “此亦但言人虽有过，犹可即此而知其厚薄，非谓必俟其有过，而后贤否可知也” — this only says that even in a person's faults one can see whether he is generous or mean; it does not mean one must wait for a fault before judging worth.
4.7.诸家: Cheng Yi: “君子常失于厚，小人常失于薄；君子过于爱，小人过于忍” — the gentleman errs on the side of generosity, the petty man on the side of meanness; the gentleman errs in loving too much, the petty man in being too hard; Yin Tun: “于此观之，则人之仁不仁可知矣” — seen this way, whether a person is humane can be known; Wu cites Wu You of the Later Han: “掾以亲故，受污辱之名，所谓观过知仁是也” — the clerk took the shame for his parent's sake; this is what “look at the fault and know the humaneness” means.
4.7.片里落点: Whether a fault leans too generous or too mean shows whether one is humane. Today: two people are half an hour late — one took a fallen old man to hospital, one overslept.

zb_say.yang: Yang takes 仁 as 人, knowing the person by the fault; Zhu keeps it as ren, seeing from each kind of fault whether one is humane.
zb_say.qian: Both gloss 党 as kind; from faults one sees generosity or meanness, warmth or hardness, and so humaneness. Qian further separates the humane heart from perfected ren; Zhu also says one need not wait for a fault to judge worth.

4.8.title: Hear the Way in the morning, die content at dusk
4.8.yw: The Master said: If one hears the Way in the morning, one may die at dusk without regret.
4.8.常见读法: Is this a heroic line about not fearing death, about dying for the truth?
4.8.字眼: zhao (morning) read zhao; “道者，事物当然之理。苟得闻之，则生顺死安，无复遗恨矣。朝夕，所以甚言其时之近” — the Way is the principle by which things ought to be; once one has truly heard it, one lives in accord and dies at peace, with nothing left to regret; “morning” and “dusk” stress how short the gap may be.
4.8.诸家: Cheng Yi: “言人不可以不知道，苟得闻道，虽死可也” — a person cannot do without knowing the Way; having heard it, even death is acceptable. Cheng Hao: “皆实理也，人知而信者为难。死生亦大矣！非诚有所得，岂以夕死为可乎” — these are all real principles; knowing them is easy, truly believing them is hard; life and death are a great matter — unless one has truly gained something, how could one call dying at dusk acceptable?
4.8.片里落点: The hard part is not hearing it but truly believing it once heard; only one who has really gained something can say “I could die that evening content.” Today: an old man in a hospital bed finally understands what he never could all his life, holds his daughter's hand and says “now I'm at peace.”

zb_say.yang: Hearing the Way matters more than staying alive; Zhu explains that one dies without regret, not that one should seek death after hearing it; Yang's translation adds no wish to die.
zb_say.qian: Both: having heard the Way one dies without regret; morning and evening stress how near. Qian stresses life's great Way and the urgency not to waste one's life; Zhu glosses the Way as the principle things ought to follow, living in accord and dying at peace.

4.9.title: A scholar set on the Way who is ashamed of poor clothes
4.9.yw: The Master said: A scholar who sets his heart on the Way, yet is ashamed of poor clothes and poor food, is not worth talking with.
4.9.常见读法: Is this telling scholars to be content with poverty?
4.9.字眼: e in “恶衣恶食” means coarse, poor; “心欲求道，而以口体之奉不若人为耻，其识趣之卑陋甚矣，何足与议于道哉” — his heart wants the Way, yet he is ashamed that the comforts of his mouth and body fall short of others': how low his sense and taste are; how could one discuss the Way with him?
4.9.诸家: Cheng Yi: “志于道而心役乎外，何足与议也” — set on the Way, yet with a heart in the service of outward things: how could one discuss anything with him?
4.9.片里落点: The mouth says the heart is set on the Way, but the heart is ordered about by things outside. The problem is not dressing poorly; it is treating poor dress as a shame. Today: someone who says he will devote himself to studying for the exam first spends three days picking the most expensive stationery.

zb_say.yang: One set on the Way who is ashamed of coarse clothes and food is not worth discussing with; Zhu explains by outward things burdening the heart and hindering talk of the Way, not by demanding that one seek poverty.
zb_say.qian: Both: shame at coarse clothes and food shows the resolve is not real and the heart serves outward things; Qian adds the scholar's social role: learning and practising the Way cannot aim at personal comfort and wealth.

4.10.title: No fixed yes, no fixed no; side with what is right
4.10.yw: The Master said: The gentleman, in dealing with the world, has no fixed yes and no fixed no; he sides with what is right.
4.10.常见读法: Is this “no principles, just see how it goes”?
4.10.字眼: di (适) read di, bi (比) read bi; Zhu Xi: “适，专主也。《春秋传》曰‘吾谁适从’是也。莫，不肯也。比，从也” — di means to insist on one thing in advance, as in the Spring and Autumn commentary “whom shall I follow?”; mo means to refuse; bi means to follow.
4.10.诸家: Zhu Xi also records Xie Liangzuo's other reading: “适，可也。莫，不可也。无可无不可，苟无道以主之，不几于猖狂自恣乎？圣人之学不然，于无可无不可之间，有义存焉” — di means “may,” mo means “may not”; with nothing either allowed or forbidden, if no Way governs it, is this not close to reckless self-indulgence? The sage's learning is otherwise: between “may” and “may not,” rightness is present. Both readings are given; the chapter closes on Xie's “rightness is present.”
4.10.片里落点: Do not decide in advance and do not refuse in advance; look only at whether it accords with what is right. “Nothing allowed, nothing forbidden” without rightness in charge is mere recklessness. Today: a line judge does not decide beforehand who should win, but bends down to see whether this one ball touched the line.

zb_say.yang: Yang explicitly adopts Zhu: 适 as insisting, 莫 as refusing, following only what is right; it is not having no judgement about anything.
zb_say.qian: Both mainly take 适 as insisting on one thing, 莫 as refusing, 比 as following: judging by rightness without fixed yes or no. Qian also keeps the reading of 适 as 敌 and 莫 as 慕 without adopting it.

4.11.title: The gentleman cherishes virtue, the petty man his comfort
4.11.yw: The Master said: The gentleman cherishes virtue, the petty man cherishes his own ground; the gentleman cherishes the law, the petty man cherishes favors.
4.11.常见读法: Is “cherishing one's ground” just homesickness, and is the petty man simply a bad person?
4.11.字眼: “怀，思念也。怀德，谓存其固有之善。怀土，谓溺其所处之安。怀刑，谓畏法。怀惠，谓贪利” — huai means to keep in mind; cherishing virtue means preserving the good one already has; cherishing one's ground means being sunk in the comfort of where one is; cherishing the law means fearing the law; cherishing favors means craving gain; “君子小人趣向不同，公私之间而已矣” — gentleman and petty man differ in where they tend, and that is only the line between public and private.
4.11.诸家: Yin Tun: “乐善恶不善，所以为君子；苟安务得，所以为小人” — delighting in good and hating what is not good makes the gentleman; settling for ease and striving for gain makes the petty man.
4.11.片里落点: “Cherishing one's ground” is not homesickness; it is a heart that guards only its own little comfort. The whole difference between gentleman and petty man lies between public and private. Today: two people receive the same job offer in another city; one asks first what he can learn and whom he can help, the other only which place is more comfortable to stay in.

zb_say.yang: Yang takes 刑 as laws and standards, not punishment only, matching Zhu's gloss of law; for 土 Yang also notes farmland, Zhu takes the place one lives at ease.
zb_say.qian: Both divide gentleman and petty man by character and what they keep in mind: virtue against settled land, fear of law against seeking favours. Qian explicitly speaks of not bearing to leave one's home soil; Zhu stresses being sunk in the comfort of one's place.

4.12.title: Act by what profits you, and resentment multiplies
4.12.yw: The Master said: One who acts by leaning on profit draws much resentment.
4.12.常见读法: Is this “trade breeds hatred,” or “profit is a bad thing”?
4.12.字眼: fang read in the rising tone, meaning to lean on; Zhu Xi cites Kong Anguo: “放，依也。多怨，谓多取怨” — fang means to rely on; much resentment means drawing much resentment onto oneself.
4.12.诸家: Cheng Yi: “欲利于己，必害于人，故多怨” — wanting profit for oneself must harm others, hence much resentment.
4.12.片里落点: The resentment does not come from the word “profit”; it comes from profiting only oneself. Today: the flatmate who never buys the shared things and uses them most finds no one seeing him off the day he moves out.

zb_say.yang: 放 read fǎng, to rely on: acting by profit easily draws resentment; Zhu glosses 放 as relying, not the 放 of giving up profit.
zb_say.qian: Qian mainly: one feels much resentment toward others; Zhu: one draws much resentment from others. Both take 放 as following, not indulging.

4.13.title: Can one govern a state with ritual and yielding?
4.13.yw: The Master said: Can one govern a state with ritual and yielding? What difficulty is there? If one cannot govern a state with ritual and yielding, what use is ritual?
4.13.常见读法: Is this “good manners and modesty can run a country,” with “ritual-yielding” read as one word?
4.13.字眼: Zhu Xi: “让者，礼之实也。何有，言不难也” — yielding is the substance of ritual; “what is there” means it is not hard; “不然，则其礼文虽具，亦且无如之何矣，而况于为国乎” — otherwise, though the forms of ritual are all in place, nothing can be done with them, let alone governing a state.
4.13.诸家: Only Zhu Xi's commentary is shown in this episode.
4.13.片里落点: Yielding is the lining inside ritual. When only the outward form is left, ritual itself no longer works, never mind governing a state. Today: a wedding banquet with every seat and formality in order, and the two families quarrel over who sits at the head table until the guests leave.

zb_say.yang: Yielding is the substance of governing and of ritual; forms alone are not enough. Yang glosses 何有 as “what difficulty?”, Zhu likewise as not hard.
zb_say.qian: Both: yielding is ritual's substance; governing by ritual and yielding is not hard; Qian stresses mutual respect and yielding above and below, rejecting ritual as a mere tool for exalting rulers over ministers.

4.14.title: Worry not about having no post, but about what you stand on
4.14.yw: The Master said: Do not worry about having no position; worry about what you would stand on in it. Do not worry that no one knows you; seek to be worth knowing.
4.14.常见读法: Is this just “don't mind if others don't understand you,” a matter of attitude?
4.14.字眼: Zhu Xi: “所以立，谓所以立乎其位者。可知，谓可以见知之实” — what one stands on means that by which one would hold the position; “worth knowing” means the real substance that could be known.
4.14.诸家: Cheng Yi: “君子求其在己者而已矣” — the gentleman seeks only what lies within himself.
4.14.片里落点: It is not about finding ways to be noticed; it is about first having the substance worth noticing. Whether a post is given, whether others know you, is not in your hands. Today: dozens of résumés with no reply; one person blames the blind employers, another redoes every project in his portfolio.

zb_say.yang: Yang, taking 立 and 位 as interchangeable, explains it as the qualifications for office; Zhu: what one stands on to hold the position. Both turn to the real substance that makes one fit for office and known, not to complaining about lacking a post.
zb_say.qian: Both value one's own talent and virtue, the substance that lets one hold a post and be known, not worrying about having no post or recognition; Qian says plainly one neither avoids office nor chases it.

4.15.title: My Way is threaded through by one
4.15.yw: The Master said: Shen! My Way is threaded through by one. Zengzi said: Yes. The Master went out, and the disciples asked: What did he mean? Zengzi said: The Master's Way is loyalty and reciprocity, nothing more.
4.15.常见读法: Is “loyalty and reciprocity” the whole content of Confucius's Way? And is “loyalty” loyalty to a ruler?
4.15.字眼: Shen (参) read shen, wei (唯) read in the rising tone; Zhu Xi: “贯，通也。唯者，应之速而无疑者也” — guan means to run through; wei is a quick answer without doubt; “尽己之谓忠，推己之谓恕” — giving one's whole self is loyalty, extending oneself to others is reciprocity; another reading: “中心为忠，如心为恕” — the heart at the center is zhong, a heart like one's own is shu.
4.15.诸家: Zhu Xi: “圣人之心，浑然一理，而泛应曲当，用各不同。曾子于其用处，盖已随事精察而力行之，但未知其体之一尔” — the sage's mind is one whole principle, responding fitly everywhere with different uses; Zengzi had already examined and practiced the uses, but did not yet know the oneness of the substance; “曾子有见于此而难言之，故借学者尽己、推己之目以著明之” — Zengzi saw this and found it hard to say, so he borrowed the learner's terms “give one's whole self” and “extend oneself” to make it plain. Cheng Yi: “圣人教人各因其才……惟曾子为能达此” — the sage teaches each according to his talent; only Zengzi could reach this.
4.15.片里落点: “Loyalty and reciprocity” do not say the Way in full; they hand the learner something to hold. “Threaded through by one” is said only to the one who is ready to understand it. Today: an old craftsman tells the apprentice just one thing: do your own step through to the end, then think of the person who takes over next.

zb_say.yang: Yang takes 忠 as establishing others as one wishes to be established, 恕 as not doing to others what one does not want; Zhu glosses 忠 as giving oneself fully and 恕 as extending oneself, linking it to one principle with many manifestations: different levels of explanation.
zb_say.qian: Both gloss 忠恕 as giving and extending oneself. Qian sees Zengzi's answer as his own grasp of the teacher's meaning, not exact but not far; Zhu says Zengzi tacitly grasped the one thread and used 忠恕 to explain it to learners: they judge his grasp differently.

4.16.title: The gentleman understands rightness; the small man understands profit
4.16.yw: The Master said: The gentleman understands rightness; the small man understands profit.
4.16.常见读法: Read as “the gentleman never speaks of profit” or “the small man is simply greedy”.
4.16.字眼: Zhu Xi: “喻，犹晓也。义者，天理之所宜。利者，人情之所欲” — yu means to understand; rightness is what Heaven's principle finds fitting; profit is what human feeling desires.
4.16.诸家: Cheng Yi: “君子之于义，犹小人之于利也。唯其深喻，是以笃好” — the gentleman stands to rightness as the small man stands to profit; because he understands it deeply, he loves it firmly. Yang Shi: “君子有舍生而取义者，以利言之……其所喻者义而已，不知利之为利故也” — a gentleman may give up his life for rightness; put in terms of profit, what he understands is rightness alone, and he does not know profit as profit.
4.16.片里落点: Both sides use the same kind of “understanding”; the difference is which thing they have understood through and through. Today: someone selling a second-hand item finds a scratch not in the listing, and changes “90% new” to “70% new” on their own.

zb_say.yang: Yang notes that it may mean those in office, the virtuous, or both, and cannot be settled; Zhu divides rightness and profit by Heaven's principle and human desire. Yang's uncertainty about status should not be flattened into a fixed class reading.
zb_say.qian: Both gloss 喻 as understanding, separating the rightness the gentleman values from the profit the petty man values; Qian explicitly refuses to define gentleman and petty man only by social position; Zhu explains by Heaven's principle and human desire.

4.17.title: Seeing a worthy, think of equalling him; seeing an unworthy, look inward
4.17.yw: The Master said: Seeing a worthy person, think of equalling him; seeing an unworthy one, turn inward and examine yourself.
4.17.常见读法: Read as “learn from role models”, with the weight falling on the other person.
4.17.字眼: Xing (省) read xǐng, to examine. Zhu Xi: “思齐者，冀己亦有是善；内自省者，恐己亦有是恶” — to think of equalling is to hope one also has that good; to examine inward is to fear one also has that fault.
4.17.诸家: Hu Yin: “见人之善恶不同，而无不反诸身者，则不徒羡人而甘自弃，不徒责人而忘自责矣” — if, seeing good and bad in others, one always turns it back on oneself, one will not merely envy others and give oneself up, nor merely blame others and forget to blame oneself.
4.17.片里落点: The people one sees are good and bad; each time, fold it back onto oneself. Today: scrolling past a peer's fine work, one person sneers “just luck”, another quietly saves the tutorial.

zb_say.yang: Seeing the worthy, think of equalling them; seeing the unworthy, examine oneself. Zhu adds that both turn back on oneself; Yang's translation does not turn it into blaming others.
zb_say.qian: Both: seeing the worthy, hope to have their good; seeing the unworthy, check oneself for their fault. Qian extends it to meeting the ancients in books; the Hu quoted by Zhu also stresses turning back on oneself, not mere envy or blame.

4.18.title: In serving parents, remonstrate gently
4.18.yw: The Master said: In serving your parents, remonstrate gently. If you see they will not follow, remain respectful and do not oppose them; labour on without resentment.
4.18.常见读法: Read as “obey one's parents”, taking “do not oppose” as “do not disagree”.
4.18.字眼: Ji (几) read jī, slight. Zhu Xi cites the Neize: “父母有过，下气怡色，柔声以谏” — when parents err, lower one's breath, soften one's face, and remonstrate in a gentle voice; “谏若不入，起敬起孝，悦则复谏” — if the remonstrance does not enter, redouble respect and filial care, and when they are pleased, remonstrate again; “与其得罪于乡党州闾，宁孰谏” — rather than let them offend the whole neighbourhood, remonstrate thoroughly.
4.18.诸家: (This episode gives only Zhu Xi and the Neize.)
4.18.片里落点: Not keeping silent, but speaking gently, and if it doesn't get through, not falling out, just trying again another time. Today: when parents forward fake ads in the family chat, one child replies “fake again,” another phones them privately and talks it through slowly.

zb_say.yang: Yang glosses 劳 as worry; Zhu ties it to not resenting even when parents are displeased or strike one. Both take 几 as gentle; 不违 does not mean stopping remonstrance.
zb_say.qian: Both: 几 is gentle; if parents do not follow, stay respectful and remonstrate again. Qian takes 见志 as the child gently showing their own intent and 劳 as worry; Zhu follows the Neize: if the remonstrance does not enter, remonstrate again, and do not resent being punished.

4.19.title: While parents live, do not travel far; if you travel, have a fixed direction
4.19.yw: The Master said: While your parents are alive, do not travel far; if you must travel, have a fixed direction.
4.19.常见读法: Read as “while parents are alive one may not leave home”.
4.19.字眼: Zhu Xi: “远游，则去亲远而为日久，定省旷而音问疏；不惟己之思亲不置，亦恐亲之念我不忘也” — travelling far means being long away from one's parents, the morning and evening greetings lapse and news grows thin; not only can one not stop thinking of them, one also fears they cannot stop thinking of oneself; “游必有方，如己告云之东，则不敢更适西，欲亲必知己之所在而无忧，召己则必至而无失也” — having a fixed direction means that if one said one was going east, one dare not switch to the west, so that the parents always know where one is and need not worry, and if they call, one will surely come.
4.19.诸家: Fan Zuyu: “子能以父母之心为心，则孝矣” — if a child can make the parents' heart his own heart, that is filial.
4.19.片里落点: If you can avoid travelling far, do; if you must go, let your parents know where you are. Today: landing on a business trip, first drop a location pin in the family group.

zb_say.yang: While parents live, do not travel far; when travelling, have a set destination. Zhu explains it as sparing parents worry and being able to return when called; not an absolute ban.
zb_say.qian: Both: travelling far may make parents miss and worry; a set direction lets them know where one is and call one back. Qian notes how modern communication and transport have changed, keeping the sense of staying in touch with parents' hearts.

4.20.title: For three years not altering his father's way
4.20.yw: The Master said: If for three years he does not alter his father's way, he may be called filial.
4.20.常见读法: Taken alone, read as “after a father dies, nothing may be changed for three years”.
4.20.字眼: Zhu Xi cites Hu Yin: “已见首篇，此盖复出而逸其半也” — this already appears in the first book; here it is repeated and has lost its first half. The chapter repeats Xue Er 1.11 without its opening, “父在，观其志；父没，观其行” (while the father lives, observe his intent; after the father dies, observe his conduct).
4.20.诸家: Under Xue Er 1.11, Zhu Xi cites Yin Tun and You Zuo: what is not in accord with the Way need not wait three years; what can be changed but can wait is left a while, to give the unbearing heart time (this episode revisits that original page).
4.20.片里落点: The half sentence must be read with the half before it; “do not alter for three years” cannot be taken alone as an iron rule. Today: when young we remember only half of what our parents said, and recall the other half only after running a household ourselves.

4.21.title: One must know the ages of one's parents
4.21.yw: The Master said: The ages of one's parents must not go unknown: on the one hand for joy, on the other for fear.
4.21.字眼: Zhu Xi: “知，犹记忆也” — to know here means to keep in memory; “常知父母之年，则既喜其寿，又惧其衰，而于爱日之诚，自有不能已者” — always knowing their ages, one is glad of their long life and fears their decline, and one's sincere cherishing of the days cannot cease.
4.21.片里落点: Joy and fear are the same fact: one more day lived is one day fewer left. Today: the phone calendar reminds you of a parent's birthday once a year, and the number grows every year.

zb_say.yang: Know your parents' ages: glad of their long life, afraid of their decline; Zhu explains joy and worry together as sincere filial cherishing of the days; Yang's translation keeps both feelings.
zb_say.qian: Both gloss 知 as always remembering the parents' age, glad of long life, fearing decline and the few days left; Qian stresses that joy and fear come together, not one after the other.

4.22.title: The ancients did not let words out, ashamed that their conduct would not keep up
4.22.yw: The Master said: The ancients did not let their words out lightly, ashamed that their own conduct would not reach them.
4.22.常见读法: Read as “speak little” or “silence is golden”.
4.22.字眼: Dai (逮) means to reach. Zhu Xi: “言古者，以见今之不然……行不及言，可耻之甚” — saying “the ancients” shows that people now are not so; conduct falling short of words is most shameful.
4.22.诸家: Fan Zuyu: “非言之难，而行之难也。人惟其不行也，是以轻言之” — it is not speaking that is hard but doing; only because people do not act do they speak lightly; “言之如其所行，行之如其所言，则出诸其口必不易矣” — if one speaks as one acts and acts as one speaks, words will not come out of the mouth easily.
4.22.片里落点: The fear is not of saying something wrong but of failing to do it. Today: in the work group chat one person replies “I'll definitely hand it in this week”; another says nothing and hands it in on Wednesday.

zb_say.yang: Caution in speaking comes from shame that deeds may not catch up; Zhu glosses 逮 as reach, Yang as catch up; it is not shame at lacking fine words.
zb_say.qian: Both: it is shameful for deeds to fall short of words, so the ancients spoke sparingly; Qian explicitly does not take 言 as writing, and Zhu also reads the chapter as about words and deeds.

4.23.title: Those who err through restraint are few
4.23.yw: The Master said: Those who go wrong through restraint are few.
4.23.常见读法: Read as “frugal people make fewer mistakes”, with restraint taken as saving money.
4.23.字眼: Xian (鲜) means few. Zhu Xi cites Xie Liangzuo: “不侈然以自放之谓约” — not letting oneself loose in extravagance is called restraint; and Yin Tun: “凡事约则鲜失，非止谓俭约也” — in all things, restraint means few errors; it does not mean thrift only.
4.23.诸家: Xie Liangzuo and Yin Tun (both cited by Zhu Xi).
4.23.片里落点: Holding back words, temper and display are all restraint, not only money. Today: the person who moves house with only two boxes is the one who loses nothing.

zb_say.yang: Yang mainly takes 约 as restraint, not thrift; Zhu cites “not letting oneself loose” and “not thrift only”, so not saving money either. Yang should not be mechanically listed as opposing Zhu here.
zb_say.qian: Both: 约 is self-restraint, not indulgence, not limited to thrift with money; Qian cites keeping to essentials in learning and work, and the Yin quoted by Zhu says plainly it is not thrift only.

4.24.title: The gentleman wishes to be slow in speech and quick in action
4.24.yw: The Master said: The gentleman wishes to be slow in speech and quick in action.
4.24.常见读法: Read as “the gentleman should talk little”, taking ne (讷) as poor speaking ability.
4.24.字眼: Ne (讷) means slow of speech. Zhu Xi cites Xie Liangzuo: “放言易，故欲讷；力行难，故欲敏” — loose talk is easy, so one wishes to be slow in it; vigorous action is hard, so one wishes to be quick in it.
4.24.诸家: Zhu Xi also cites Hu Yin: “自吾道一贯至此十章，疑皆曾子门人所记也” — the ten chapters from “my Way is threaded through by one” to here were perhaps all recorded by Zengzi's disciples. This is a conjecture, and Zhu Xi records it without settling it.
4.24.片里落点: Of the easy end and the hard end, rein in the easy one (speaking) and spur on the hard one (doing). It is not refusing to speak, but not talking loosely.

zb_say.yang: Careful in speech, quick in action; Yang explains by “quick in affairs, careful in speech” from Xue Er, Zhu by speech being hard and action wanting to be easy; it does not praise sluggishness.
zb_say.qian: Both: speech should be careful, action diligent, correcting loose talk and slow deeds. Qian explains it as changing one's temperament by practice; Zhu cites Xie: loose talk is easy, vigorous action hard.

4.25.title: Virtue is not solitary; it is sure to have neighbours
4.25.yw: The Master said: Virtue is not solitary; it is sure to have neighbours.
4.25.常见读法: Read as a consolation: “good people are never alone”.
4.25.字眼: Zhu Xi: “邻，犹亲也。德不孤立，必以类应。故有德者，必有其类从之，如居之有邻也” — neighbour means those close to one; virtue does not stand alone but is answered by its kind; so one who has virtue will have his kind follow him, as a dwelling has neighbours.
4.25.片里落点: This is not “good deeds are rewarded”; it is like answering like. What you hold to draws people who hold to the same thing.

zb_say.yang: The virtuous will have kindred who draw close; Yang cites “like sounds and like breath seek each other”, Zhu glosses 邻 as those close, virtue not standing alone; it does not promise an actual post.
zb_say.qian: Both: the virtuous are answered by kindred and are not alone. Qian also lists the view that virtue needs teachers and friends to support it, without adopting it.

4.26.title: Importune a ruler and you meet disgrace; importune a friend and you grow distant
4.26.yw: Ziyou said: In serving a ruler, importunity brings disgrace; among friends, importunity brings distance.
4.26.常见读法: Read as “don't keep bothering your boss or friends”, or reading shu (数) as “to scold”.
4.26.字眼: Shuo (数) read shuò, frequent. Zhu Xi cites the Cheng brothers: “数，烦数也” — shuo means tiresome frequency; and Hu Yin: “事君谏不行，则当去；导友善不纳，则当止” — when remonstrance with a ruler is not acted on, one should leave; when guiding a friend to good is not accepted, one should stop.
4.26.诸家: Fan Zuyu: “君臣朋友，皆以义合，故其事同也” — ruler and minister, friend and friend, are all joined by rightness, so the matter is the same. These are Ziyou's words.
4.26.片里落点: Persuasion has limits. When it does not get through, stop (with a ruler, leave); urging too often only pushes people away.

zb_say.yang: Yang glosses 数 as repeatedly, rendering it freely as fussy; Zhu as tiresomely often. Both mean pressing remonstrance on a ruler or friend too often brings disgrace or distance; it does not excuse failing to advise.
zb_say.qian: Both read 数 as tiresome pressing: remonstrating with a ruler or guiding a friend too insistently brings disgrace and distance. Qian also keeps the reading of 数 as listing faults without adopting it; the Hu quoted by Zhu stresses leaving or stopping when not heeded.

5.1.title: Gongye Chang is fit to be given a wife
5.1.yw: The Master said of Gongye Chang: He is fit to be given a wife. Though he was in bonds, it was not his crime. And he gave him his own daughter as wife. The Master said of Nan Rong: When the state has the Way, he will not be cast aside; when the state lacks the Way, he will escape punishment. And he gave him his elder brother's daughter as wife.
5.1.常见读法: Confucius married his daughter to a man who had been in prison: read as “he did not mind” or “he was broad-minded”.
5.1.字眼: Qi (妻) in the falling tone: to give a daughter in marriage. “缧，黑索也。绁，挛也” — lei is a black rope, xie is a binding; “长之为人无所考，而夫子称其可妻，其必有以取之矣” — nothing is known of Chang's character, but since the Master called him fit to marry, there must have been something to recommend him; “夫有罪无罪，在我而已，岂以自外至者为荣辱哉” — guilt or innocence lies in oneself alone; how could what comes from outside be one's honour or shame? On Nan Rong: “不废，言必见用也……以其谨于言行” — not cast aside means he will surely be employed, because he was careful in word and deed.
5.1.诸家: The Cheng brothers reject the “avoiding suspicion” reading: “此以己之私心窥圣人也。凡人避嫌者，皆内不足也……嫁女必量其才而求配” — this is to peer at the sage with one's own selfish mind; all who avoid suspicion are lacking within; in marrying a daughter one must weigh a man's ability and seek a match.
5.1.片里落点: What matters is that the crime was not his; a prison imposed from outside is no measure of his honour. Today: someone was wrongly disciplined and later cleared; some people avoid him, and some still hand him the important jobs.

zb_say.yang: Yang 5.1: same reading: 缧绁 is imprisonment, not his crime, so one may give him a daughter; Zhu says honour and disgrace cannot be judged by outward misfortune; Yang's note does not include the legend that he understood birds. Yang 5.2: same reading: Nan Rong would be employed in good times and escape harm in bad; the bride was Confucius's elder brother's daughter. Zhu joins this with the Gongye Chang chapter; Yang makes it a separate chapter.
zb_say.qian: Both: 缧绁 is the rope binding prisoners; not his crime, so he may still marry the daughter. Nan Rong was careful in word and deed and would escape punishment, so he was given the brother's daughter. Qian does not rank Gongye Chang and Nan Rong by daughter versus niece; Zhu also rejects that.

5.2.title: Of Zijian the Master said: A gentleman indeed is this man
5.2.yw: The Master said of Zijian: A gentleman indeed is this man! If Lu had no gentlemen, where could he have got this from?
5.2.常见读法: Read only as one line of praise for Zijian.
5.2.字眼: Yan (焉) read yān. Zijian's surname is Fu (宓, read fú), personal name Buqi. “上斯斯此人，下斯斯此德” — the first si refers to this man, the second to this virtue; “子贱盖能尊贤取友以成其德者……因以见鲁之多贤也” — Zijian honoured the worthy and chose friends to complete his virtue; this also shows how many worthies Lu had.
5.2.诸家: Su Shi (cited by Zhu Xi): “称人之善，必本其父兄师友，厚之至也” — in praising someone's goodness, to root it in his father, brothers, teachers and friends is the height of generosity.
5.2.片里落点: A person's virtue is taken from the worthies around him, so praising him means also praising those who made him. Today: a newcomer wins an award and the first thing said on stage is to point to a teacher in the audience.

zb_say.qian: Both: the first 斯 refers to the man, the second to the virtue; Zijian is praised for honouring the worthy and choosing friends to complete his virtue, which also shows that Lu had many worthies.

5.3.title: Zigong asked: What about me?
5.3.yw: Zigong asked: What about me, Ci? The Master said: You are a vessel. He said: What vessel? He said: A hu-lian vessel of the ancestral temple.
5.3.常见读法: Calling Zigong a “vessel” is read as a put-down, since “the gentleman is not a vessel”.
5.3.字眼: Ru (女) read rǔ, “you”; hulian (瑚琏) read hú liǎn. “器者，有用之成材” — a vessel is a finished, useful material; the hulian is “宗庙盛黍稷之器而饰以玉，器之贵重而华美者也” — a temple vessel for millet, adorned with jade, the most precious and beautiful of vessels; “子贡虽未至于不器，其亦器之贵者欤” — though Zigong had not reached “not being a vessel”, he was a precious one among vessels.
5.3.诸家: Zhu Xi gives a single reading only.
5.3.片里落点: Two layers in one line: not yet “not a vessel”, but the most precious kind of vessel; praise with direction in it. Today: the boss says “you're the most useful person on my team”, and it feels good at the time but not quite right on the way home.

zb_say.qian: Both gloss 瑚琏 as a precious, beautiful temple vessel for grain. Qian does not bring in the “gentleman is not a vessel” chapter; Zhu explicitly says Zigong had not reached “not a vessel” but was a precious vessel.

5.4.title: Yong is humane but not glib
5.4.yw: Someone said: Yong is humane but not glib. The Master said: What use is glibness? Those who meet people with a ready tongue are often disliked. I do not know whether he is humane, but what use is glibness?
5.4.常见读法: Read as “poor speakers lose out, so train your eloquence”.
5.4.字眼: “佞，口才也” — ning is a talent for speech; Zhonggong was “重厚简默，而时人以佞为贤” — weighty, simple and quiet, while people of the time thought glibness a virtue; “御，当也，犹应答也。给，辩也。憎，恶也” — yu is to meet, as in replying; ji is ready argument; zeng is to dislike; “佞人所以应答人者，但以口取辩而无情实，徒多为人所憎恶尔” — the glib answer people with argument from the mouth but no real substance, and only win much dislike; “其不佞乃所以为贤，不足以为病也。再言焉用佞，所以深晓之” — his not being glib is exactly his worth, not a flaw; saying “what use is glibness” twice is to make it deeply clear.
5.4.诸家: Zhu Xi on why Confucius would not grant him humaneness: “仁道至大，非全体而不息者，不足以当之。如颜子亚圣，犹不能无违于三月之后” — the way of humaneness is very great; only one whole and unceasing can match it; even Yan Hui, second to the sage, could not avoid lapsing after three months.
5.4.片里落点: The root problem is “no real substance”: a quick, argumentative tongue with nothing true in it wins more dislike the more it talks. Confucius did not grant Zhonggong humaneness because humaneness is too great to grant lightly. Today: the person who takes on everything, agrees to everything and delivers nothing finds colleagues walking around him three months later.

zb_say.qian: Both: 佞 is a talent for speech; answering people with a ready tongue easily breeds dislike, and the judgement of ren must not be granted lightly. Qian stresses that lacking eloquence is no fault in Zhonggong; Zhu says the same.

5.5.title: The Master wished Qidiao Kai to take office
5.5.yw: The Master wished Qidiao Kai to take office. He replied: I am not yet able to be sure of this. The Master was pleased.
5.5.常见读法: Declining office read as modesty or lack of nerve.
5.5.字眼: Yue (说) read yuè, pleased. “斯，指此理而言。信，谓真知其如此，而无毫发之疑也” — si refers to this principle; to be sure is to know truly that it is so, without a hair of doubt; “开自言未能如此，未可以治人，故夫子说其笃志” — Kai said he could not yet do so and was not fit to govern others, so the Master was pleased at the firmness of his aim.
5.5.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “漆雕开已见大意，故夫子说之” — Qidiao Kai had seen the main idea, so the Master was pleased. Xie Liangzuo: “至于心术之微，则一毫不自得，不害其为未信。此圣人所不能知，而开自知之。其材可以仕，而其器不安于小成” — in the subtle workings of the mind, a hair not truly gained is enough to make him not yet sure; this the sage could not know, but Kai knew it himself; his talent was fit for office, but his capacity would not rest in small achievement.
5.5.片里落点: Whether one's ability is enough, a teacher can see; the hair-thin part not truly gained inside, only oneself knows. Admitting that hair is refusing to rest in small achievement, so Confucius was glad. Today: offered a promotion, she says she can't carry that role yet and asks for another six months.

zb_say.qian: Qian connects it to taking office: not yet confident of practising the Way, he wished to study further; Zhu: this principle, not yet known truly beyond doubt. Both explain the Master's pleasure by firm resolve not content with small success.

5.6.title: If the Way does not prevail, I will take a raft out to sea
5.6.yw: The Master said: If the Way does not prevail, I will board a raft and float out to sea. The one who would follow me would be Yóu, perhaps? Zilu heard this and was glad. The Master said: Yóu loves courage more than I do, but has nothing by which to measure things.
5.6.常见读法: Read as Confucius really wanting to retire overseas; or wu suo qu cai (无所取材) as “nowhere to get timber”.
5.6.字眼: “桴，筏也” — fu is a raft; hao (好) in the falling tone; “材，与裁同，古字借用” — cai is the same as cai “to measure”, an ancient borrowed character; “子路勇于义，故谓其能从己，皆假设之言耳。子路以为实然……讥其不能裁度事理，以适于义也” — Zilu was brave for rightness, so he was said to be able to follow; these were all hypothetical words. Zilu took them literally, and was chided for being unable to weigh the matter to fit rightness.
5.6.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “浮海之叹，伤天下之无贤君也” — the sigh about floating out to sea is grief that the world has no worthy ruler.
5.6.片里落点: Going out to sea is a sigh, a figure of speech; Zilu took it literally, with courage to spare but no sense of measuring what is fitting. Today: someone in the group chat says offhand they'll quit and travel the world, and someone else packs a bag that very night.

zb_say.qian: Qian mainly takes 材 as the bamboo and wood for the raft: nothing to rely on for practising the Way; Zhu takes it as 裁, weighing: Zilu could not weigh matters to fit rightness.

5.7.title: Meng Wubo asked whether Zilu was humane
5.7.yw: Meng Wubo asked: Is Zilu humane? The Master said: I do not know. He asked again. The Master said: You could be put in charge of the levies of a state of a thousand chariots; I do not know whether he is humane. What about Qiu? The Master said: Qiu could be made steward of a town of a thousand households or a house of a hundred chariots; I do not know whether he is humane. What about Chi? The Master said: Chi, with his sash tied, standing at court, could be made to speak with guests; I do not know whether he is humane.
5.7.常见读法: Confucius refusing to rate his students read as protectiveness or modesty.
5.7.字眼: Sheng (乘) read shèng; “赋，兵也。古者以田赋出兵，故谓兵为赋” — fu means troops; in antiquity troops were levied by land tax, so troops were called fu; “宰，邑长家臣之通号” — zai is the general title of a town head or household steward; chao (朝) read cháo; “子路之于仁，盖日月至焉者，或在或亡，不能必其有无，故以不知告之” — Zilu reached humaneness for a day or a month, sometimes present, sometimes absent, and it could not be guaranteed, so Confucius answered “I do not know”; “言子路之才，可见者如此，仁则不能知也” — he spoke of what Zilu's ability visibly was; humaneness could not be known.
5.7.诸家: Zhu Xi gives a single reading only.
5.7.片里落点: Say plainly what visible ability there is; humaneness comes and goes, and one does not vouch for it. Three students, three talents: each line says what they can do, none says they are humane. Today: in a background check, the referee says “I vouch for his skills; his character I can't speak to”.

zb_say.qian: Both separate visible ability in government from ren, which cannot be granted lightly; managing 赋 means military affairs, and 宰 and receiving guests are glossed alike; not knowing their ren does not deny their talent.

5.8.title: Who is better, you or Hui?
5.8.yw: The Master said to Zigong: Who is better, you or Hui? He replied: How would I dare to look up to Hui? Hui hears one thing and knows ten; I hear one thing and know two. The Master said: You are not his equal. I grant that you are not his equal.
5.8.常见读法: Wu yu ru fu ru ye (吾与女弗如也) read as “neither you nor I is his equal”, Confucius being modest.
5.8.字眼: Ru (女) read rǔ; “愈，胜也” — yu means better; “一，数之始。十，数之终。二者，一之对也。颜子明睿所照，即始而见终；子贡推测而知，因此而识彼” — one is the beginning of numbers, ten the end, two the counterpart of one; Yan Hui's clear insight saw the end from the beginning; Zigong knew by inference, recognising that from this; “与，许也” — yu means to grant.
5.8.诸家: Zhu Xi cites Hu Yin: “子贡方人，夫子既语以不暇，又问其与回孰愈，以观其自知之如何” — Zigong liked comparing people; the Master had told him he had no time for that, and then asked who was better, he or Hui, to see how well he knew himself; “夫子以其自知之明，而又不难于自屈，故既然之，又重许之” — because he knew himself clearly and did not find it hard to yield, the Master both agreed and emphatically granted it.
5.8.片里落点: Confucius's question tests whether Zigong sees himself clearly. He does, and does not find it hard to bow, so Confucius first says “you are not his equal” and then solemnly affirms him. Today: a coach asks two players who is stronger, and one points at the other without a second thought.

zb_say.qian: The 与 of 吾与女弗如也 differs: Qian takes it as “and”: you and I are both not as good as Hui; Zhu takes it as “grant”: approving Zigong's knowing he falls short. The contrast between seeing the whole from one and inferring the other from this is close.

5.9.title: Zai Yu slept in the daytime
5.9.yw: Zai Yu slept in the daytime. The Master said: Rotten wood cannot be carved; a wall of dung cannot be plastered. As for Yu, what is the use of scolding him? The Master said: At first, with people, I heard their words and trusted their conduct. Now, with people, I hear their words and watch their conduct. It was Yu who made me change.
5.9.常见读法: Read as Confucius scolding a student far too harshly over a nap.
5.9.字眼: “昼寝，谓当昼而寐” — daytime sleeping means sleeping in broad day; “朽，腐也。雕，刻画也。杇，镘也” — xiu is rotten, diao is to carve, wu (杇, read wū) is to plaster; “言其志气昏惰，教无所施也” — his will and spirit were dull and idle, so teaching had nothing to work on; “与，语辞。诛，责也。言不足责，乃所以深责之” — yu is a particle; zhu means to rebuke; saying he is not worth rebuking is the deepest rebuke; xing (行) in the falling tone; “宰予能言而行不逮，故孔子自言于予之事而改此失，亦以重警之也” — Zai Yu spoke well but his conduct fell short, so Confucius said that through Yu he had corrected this fault, also to warn him severely.
5.9.诸家: Hu Yin: “子曰疑衍文，不然，则非一日之言也” — the second “the Master said” may be an interpolation; otherwise these were words of different days. Fan Zuyu: “君子之于学，惟日孜孜，毙而后已……宰予昼寝，自弃孰甚焉” — the gentleman in learning is diligent every day until death; Zai Yu sleeping in the day — what self-abandonment is greater? Hu Yin: “宰予不能以志帅气，居然而倦。是宴安之气胜，儆戒之志惰也” — Zai Yu could not lead his vital spirit with his will and grew weary; the spirit of ease won and the will to vigilance slackened; “特因此立教，以警群弟子，使谨于言而敏于行耳” — Confucius merely used this to set a teaching and warn all his disciples to be careful in word and quick in deed.
5.9.片里落点: The point is not the nap but a slackened will and words that deeds do not match. “Not worth rebuking” is the heaviest rebuke. Confucius used the occasion to set a rule: hear the words, and also watch the conduct. Today: three gym memberships in a year, and not one visit.

zb_say.qian: Both: 昼寝 is sleeping by day; rotten wood and a dung wall image a dull, idle spirit that teaching cannot work on. Neither adopts the “painting the bedroom” reading; the second half uses listening to words and watching deeds to correct speaking well while deeds lag.

5.10.title: I have never seen anyone who is truly firm
5.10.yw: The Master said: I have never seen anyone who is truly firm. Someone answered: Shen Cheng. The Master said: Cheng has desires; how can he be firm?
5.10.常见读法: Taking a hard temper and refusing to yield to anyone as “firmness”.
5.10.字眼: Cheng (枨) read chéng; yan (焉) read yān; “刚，坚强不屈之意，最人所难能者” — firmness means strong and unbending, the hardest thing for people to manage; “欲，多嗜欲也。多嗜欲，则不得为刚矣” — desire means many cravings; with many cravings one cannot be firm.
5.10.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “人有欲则无刚，刚则不屈于欲” — with desires one has no firmness; the firm do not bend to desire. Xie Liangzuo: “刚与欲正相反。能胜物之谓刚，故常伸于万物之上；为物揜之谓欲，故常屈于万物之下” — firmness and desire are exact opposites; being able to overcome things is firmness, so it always stands above all things; being covered by things is desire, so it always bends beneath them; “其为人得非悻悻自好者乎？故或者疑以为刚，然不知此其所以为欲尔” — was he not a prickly, self-regarding man? So some took him for firm, not knowing that this was exactly his desire.
5.10.片里落点: Firmness holds things down; desire is being covered by things. Looking hard and loving to win may mean being led by one's own desires. Today: the person who speaks most aggressively in meetings and yields to no one cannot walk past a mall sale.

zb_say.qian: Both: 刚 is not bending to outside things; with many cravings one cannot be firm. Qian notes that having no desires is not the same as being firm, avoiding inferring a sufficient condition from a necessary one.

5.11.title: What I do not wish others to do to me
5.11.yw: Zigong said: What I do not wish others to do to me, I also wish not to do to others. The Master said: Ci, that is not something you have reached.
5.11.常见读法: Read as another version of “do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself”, something anyone can do.
5.11.字眼: “子贡言我所不欲人加于我之事，我亦不欲以此加之于人。此仁者之事，不待勉强，故夫子以为非子贡所及” — Zigong said that what he did not want others to do to him, he did not want to do to others; this is the work of the humane, needing no effort, so the Master judged it beyond Zigong; “愚谓无者自然而然，勿者禁止之谓，此所以为仁恕之别” — in my view, wu (无, there is none) is what happens of itself, wu (勿, do not) is prohibition; this is the difference between humaneness and reciprocity.
5.11.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “我不欲人之加诸我，吾亦欲无加诸人，仁也；施诸己而不愿，亦勿施于人，恕也。恕则子贡或能勉之，仁则非所及矣” — what I do not want done to me, I also wish there to be none of from me to others: that is humaneness; what one would not want done to oneself, do not do to others: that is reciprocity. Reciprocity Zigong might manage with effort; humaneness is beyond him.
5.11.片里落点: The difference is between “not” and “do not”: having no such wish in the first place is ren; having it and holding yourself back is shu. Today: you hate being woken by messages at midnight, so you schedule anything after 10 pm to send the next morning.

zb_say.qian: Qian weighs the first line: one cannot ensure others will not wrong one; Zhu weighs the second: doing no wrong to others is natural to the humane, needs no effort, and is beyond Zigong.

5.12.title: The Master's outward cultivation can be heard
5.12.yw: Zigong said: The Master's outward cultivation we may hear about; the Master's words on human nature and the Way of Heaven we may not hear about.
5.12.常见读法: Read as Zigong complaining that Confucius never spoke of nature and the Way of Heaven, or that Confucius did not discuss metaphysics at all.
5.12.字眼: “文章，德之见乎外者，威仪文辞皆是也” — wenzhang is virtue showing outwardly: bearing and speech are both it; “性者，人所受之天理；天道者，天理自然之本体，其实一理也” — nature is the heavenly principle a person receives; the Way of Heaven is the natural substance of that principle; in truth they are one principle; “盖圣门教不躐等，子贡至是始得闻之，而叹其美也” — the sage's school did not teach out of order; only now did Zigong get to hear it, and he sighed at its beauty.
5.12.诸家: The Cheng brothers: “此子贡闻夫子之至论而叹美之言也” — these are Zigong's words of admiration on hearing the Master's highest teaching.
5.12.片里落点: “Wenzhang” is virtue showing in words and conduct; Confucius seldom spoke of nature and the Way of Heaven, and Zigong hearing it for the first time is admiration, not complaint. Today: after an apprentice has chopped vegetables in the kitchen for three years, the old chef finally talks to her about heat.

zb_say.qian: The point differs: Qian holds Zigong truly sighs that nature and Heaven's Way could not be heard, 文章 being the Odes, Documents, ritual and music; Zhu holds Zigong only now heard them and praised them, 文章 being virtue showing outwardly in bearing and speech.

5.13.title: When Zilu heard something
5.13.yw: When Zilu had heard something and had not yet been able to put it into practice, he only feared hearing something more.
5.13.常见读法: Read as Zilu being afraid to learn new things, as if he disliked learning.
5.13.字眼: “前所闻者既未及行，故恐复有所闻而行之不给也” — what he had heard before was not yet carried out, so he feared hearing more and not having time to carry it out (ji 给 read jǐ: to be in time).
5.13.诸家: Fan Zuyu: “子路闻善，勇于必行，门人自以为弗及也，故著之。若子路，可谓能用其勇矣” — when Zilu heard of good he was bold to carry it out; his fellow disciples felt they could not match him, so they recorded it; one like Zilu may be said to use his courage well.
5.13.片里落点: What he feared was not learning more, but the last thing not yet done. His fellow students recorded it because they felt they fell short. Today: one course not yet practised through, so don't sign up for the next.

zb_say.qian: Both: fearing to hear more before acting on what he had heard shows Zilu's boldness in action, fearing he could not keep up; both see it recorded to show his worth, not as opposing further learning.

5.14.title: Why was Kong Wenzi called “wen”?
5.14.yw: Zigong asked: Why was Kong Wenzi called “wen”? The Master said: He was quick and loved learning, and was not ashamed to ask those below him; that is why he was called “wen”.
5.14.常见读法: Read “not ashamed to ask those below” as a general virtue of diligence, unrelated to Kong Wenzi's character.
5.14.字眼: “凡人性敏者多不好学，位高者多耻下问。故谥法有以勤学好问为文者，盖亦人所难也” — people quick by nature mostly do not love learning, and those of high rank are mostly ashamed to ask those below; so the rules for posthumous names count diligent learning and asking as “wen”, for it is hard for people; “孔子不没其善，言能如此，亦足以为文矣，非经天纬地之文也” — Confucius did not bury his good points; being able to do this is enough for “wen”, though not the “wen” that orders heaven and earth.
5.14.诸家: Zhu Xi cites a Master Su on Kong Wenzi's deeds — having Taishu Ji put away his wife, then wanting to attack him, and Confucius ordering his carriage and leaving: “其为人如此而谥曰文，此子贡之所以疑而问也” — such was the man, yet he was named “wen”; that is why Zigong doubted and asked.
5.14.片里落点: Confucius answers only with the one line of the posthumous-name rules, “quick and fond of learning, not ashamed to ask those below,” without defending Kong Wenzi wholesale. Today: a boss with an ordinary reputation asks the intern in front of everyone, “I don't understand this, can you explain?”

zb_say.qian: Both: quickness, love of learning and not being ashamed to ask those below justify the name 文; private faults do not erase the good. Qian says “below” is not limited to rank or age; Zhu stresses that the quick-witted and highly placed rarely love learning and ask below.

5.15.title: Zichan had four ways of the gentleman
5.15.yw: The Master said of Zichan: He had four ways of the gentleman. In conducting himself he was respectful; in serving his superiors he was reverent; in nourishing the people he was kind; in employing the people he was just.
5.15.常见读法: Read as Confucius praising Zichan point by point, showing Zichan was perfect.
5.15.字眼: “恭，谦逊也。敬，谨恪也。惠，爱利也” — gong is modesty, jing is carefulness, hui is loving benefit; “使民义，如都鄙有章，上下有服，田有封洫，庐井有伍之类” — employing the people justly means such things as capital and outlying districts having their rules, upper and lower having their garments, fields having boundaries and ditches, and households being grouped in fives.
5.15.诸家: Wu Yu: “数其事而责之者，其所善者多也……数其事而称之者，犹有所未至也……今或以一言盖一人，一事盖一时，皆非也” — when one lists someone's deeds to blame him, his good points are many; when one lists his deeds to praise him, there is still something he has not reached; now to sum up a person in one phrase, or an age in one event, is always wrong.
5.15.片里落点: Praising point by point actually shows there is still somewhere he has not reached. Respectful to himself, reverent to superiors, kind to the people, just in employing them: each of the four has its own object. Judging a person by one phrase or one event is wrong. Today: don't judge a small shop open for thirty years by one bad review.

zb_say.qian: The glosses of 恭敬惠义 are the same. Qian does not dwell on what Zichan fell short of because four merits are listed; Zhu also cites Wu: listing someone's merits also shows what he lacked; the evaluation leans slightly differently.

5.16.title: Is it more polite not to stand on ceremony with old friends?
5.16.yw: The Master said: Yan Pingzhong was good at associating with others; long acquainted, he still treated them with respect.
5.16.常见读法: Once you have known someone a long time you no longer need formalities; being polite only keeps them at a distance.
5.16.字眼: “久而敬之” — long acquainted, still respectful.
5.16.诸家: Zhu Xi: “晏平仲，齐大夫，名婴” — Yan Pingzhong, a grandee of Qi, personal name Ying. He cites Master Cheng: “人交久则敬衰，久而能敬，所以为善” — when people have known each other long, respect fades; to keep respect after a long time is what makes him good at it.
5.16.片里落点: Respect fading with time is the usual course; keeping it is what “good at associating with others” means. Today: after five years sharing a flat, a roommate still knocks before borrowing your charger.

zb_say.qian: Both: Yan Pingzhong, however long he knew people, still respected them; 敬之 is not read as the outward effect of others respecting Yan.

5.17.title: Was Zang Wenzhong really clever?
5.17.yw: The Master said: Zang Wenzhong housed a great tortoise, with hills carved on the capitals and water-weeds painted on the king-posts. How can he be called wise?
5.17.常见读法: Zang Wenzhong was learned and widely informed, and everyone at the time thought him clever.
5.17.字眼: “居，犹藏也。蔡，大龟也” — “ju” means to store; “Cai” is a great tortoise; “节，柱头斗栱” — “jie” are the bracket sets on the column heads; “梲，梁上短柱” — “zhuo” are the short posts on the beams; “知” is read as “zhi”, wisdom.
5.17.诸家: Zhu Xi: “不务民义，而谄渎鬼神如此，安得为知” — not attending to what is right for the people, but flattering and profaning spirits like this — how could he be wise?; “春秋传所谓作虚器，即此事也” — what the Zuo Commentary calls “making empty vessels” is this very affair. He cites Zhang Zai: “山节藻梲为藏龟之室，祀爰居之义，同归于不知宜矣” — the carved chamber for the tortoise and the sacrifice to the yuanju bird come to the same thing: not knowing what is fitting.
5.17.片里落点: Not putting his mind to what the people needed, and courting spirits instead, does not count as wisdom. Today: business is slow, and instead of asking customers, the owner spends a fortune turning the shop door to face another way.

zb_say.qian: Both: 居蔡 is keeping a great tortoise; the carved brackets and posts adorned its chamber; not attending to the people's due and flattering spirits for blessings, he cannot be called wise. Qian also notes the carvings were originally ornaments of the royal temple.

5.18.title: Not even this counts as ren?
5.18.yw: Zizhang asked: Prime Minister Ziwen took office as prime minister three times without a look of joy, and was dismissed three times without a look of resentment. He always told the new prime minister about the affairs of the old. What do you think of him? The Master said: He was loyal. — Was he ren? — I do not know; how could he be ren? — When Cuizi killed the lord of Qi, Chen Wenzi had ten teams of horses; he gave them up and left. On reaching another state he said: “They are like our grandee Cuizi,” and left. On reaching another state he again said: “They are like our grandee Cuizi,” and left. What do you think of him? The Master said: He was pure. — Was he ren? — I do not know; how could he be ren?
5.18.常见读法: Taking office three times without joy, dismissed three times without resentment, and abandoning his fortune to leave a disordered state — how could that not be ren?
5.18.字眼: “三已之” — “yi” means to be dismissed; “十乘，四十匹” — ten teams are forty horses; “违，去也” — “wei” means to leave; in “未知，焉得仁” the “知” keeps its ordinary reading, to know.
5.18.诸家: Zhu Xi: of Ziwen, “但许其忠，而未许其仁” — he granted only his loyalty, not his ren; of Wenzi, “特许其清，而不许其仁” — he granted only his purity, not his ren. He cites his teacher: “当理而无私心，则仁矣” — to accord with principle with no selfish mind, that is ren; “子张未识仁体，而悦于苟难，遂以小者信其大者” — Zizhang did not yet know the substance of ren and was taken with hard feats, so he trusted the small to vouch for the great; “以他书考之” — checking other books, Ziwen “所谋者无非僭王猾夏之事” — all he planned was usurping the royal title and troubling the central states, and Wenzi “不数岁而复反于齐” — within a few years went back to Qi.
5.18.片里落点: Loyalty and purity are single virtues; ren asks whether one fully accords with principle and truly has no selfish mind. Trusting small things to vouch for great ones was Zizhang's fault. Today: leaving a job with a clean handover, even the password book left behind, is loyalty to duty — no more than that yet.

zb_say.qian: Neither grants complete ren for one act of loyalty or purity. Qian takes 未知 as tactful and strictly separates one virtue from complete virtue; Zhu says ren is not granted because it is unknown whether the motive was pure principle without selfish desire.

5.19.title: Why is thinking twice enough?
5.19.yw: Ji Wenzi thought three times before he acted. When the Master heard of it, he said: Twice is enough.
5.19.常见读法: “Think three times before you act” is usually praised as a virtue, so why did Confucius say twice was enough?
5.19.字眼: “三” here is read sàn, meaning “again and again”; “斯，语辞” — “si” is a particle.
5.19.诸家: Zhu Xi: Ji Wenzi “每事必三思而后行，若使晋而求遭丧之礼以行” — thought three times before every act, as when, sent to Jin, he first sought out the rites for a death in mourning. He cites Master Cheng: “再则已审，三则私意起而反惑矣” — by the second time it is already clear; by the third, selfish thoughts arise and confuse instead. Zhu Xi adds that when Duke Xuan usurped the throne, Wenzi “不能讨，反为之使齐而纳赂焉” — could not punish him and instead went to Qi on his behalf with bribes: “君子务穷理而贵果断，不徒多思之为尚” — the gentleman works to understand fully and values decisiveness, not mere quantity of thought.
5.19.片里落点: By the second time it is already clear; by the third, self-interest creeps in. Today: a contract is clear after two readings; by the fourth, you start finding faults that aren't faults.

zb_say.qian: Both: by the second thought it is clear; thinking more adds selfish thoughts and confusion; mere quantity of thought is not praised. Qian lays out two readings and chooses this from Ji Wenzi's conduct; Zhu cites Cheng and the bribery episode as proof.

5.20.title: Why is this “foolishness” harder to learn than cleverness?
5.20.yw: The Master said: When the state had the Way, Ning Wuzi was wise; when it lacked the Way, he was foolish. His wisdom can be matched; his foolishness cannot.
5.20.常见读法: “His foolishness cannot be matched” is used today as an insult — so why is this kind of foolishness harder to learn than cleverness?
5.20.字眼: “知” is read as “zhi”, wisdom; “甯” is read nìng.
5.20.诸家: Zhu Xi: Ning Wuzi “仕卫，当文公、成公之时” — served Wei under Dukes Wen and Cheng; under Duke Wen, who had the Way, “无事可见，此其知之可及也” — there was nothing remarkable to see, so his wisdom could be matched; under Duke Cheng, who lacked the Way and lost the state, he “周旋其间，尽心竭力，不避艰险……而能卒保其身以济其君，此其愚之不可及也” — moved through it all, giving his whole heart and strength, not avoiding danger, and in the end kept himself safe and rescued his lord; that is the foolishness that cannot be matched. He cites Master Cheng: “邦无道能沉晦以免患……亦有不当愚者，比干是也” — when the state lacks the Way one may keep a low profile to avoid harm, yet there are some who should not play the fool, such as Bi Gan.
5.20.片里落点: The “foolishness” is taking on what every clever person avoids, while still keeping himself safe and saving his lord; Master Cheng's mention of Bi Gan shows it is not simply feigning stupidity. Today: the year the company hit trouble everyone left, and she stayed to sort out the bad books.

zb_say.qian: Both: in bad times seeming foolish while preserving oneself and saving the ruler is hard to match. Qian leans to self-concealment, not merely saving oneself; Zhu first speaks of giving all one's effort in the thick of it and also cites Cheng on lying low to avoid harm.

5.21.title: After so many years of travel, what did Confucius go home to do?
5.21.yw: When the Master was in Chen he said: Let us go home! Let us go home! The young men of my village are ambitious and careless; they have produced something of real pattern, but do not know how to cut it to shape.
5.21.常见读法: After so many years travelling the states, what did Confucius go home to do?
5.21.字眼: “与” is read yú, a particle; “斐” is read fěi; “裁，割正也” — “cai” means to cut straight; “狂简，志大而略于事” — “ambitious and careless” means great aims but little attention to practical affairs.
5.21.诸家: Zhu Xi: “此孔子周流四方，道不行而思归之叹也” — this is Confucius' sigh of longing for home after wandering everywhere without his Way being put into practice; “夫子初心，欲行其道于天下，至是而知其终不用也。于是始欲成就后学，以传道于来世” — his original wish was to practise the Way across the world; by now he knew he would never be employed, so he began to want to form his students and pass the Way on to later ages; “不得中行之士而思其次……但恐其过中失正，而或陷于异端耳，故欲归而裁之也” — not finding men of the middle way, he thought of the next best, only fearing they would overshoot the mean and fall into heterodoxy, so he wanted to go home and shape them.
5.21.片里落点: He turns from practising the Way to transmitting it; ambitious young men can advance in the Way, but risk overshooting, so he goes home to trim them. Today: a new hire's proposal has eight good ideas in ten pages, and still needs someone to help cut it down.

zb_say.qian: Both: the Way not practised, he longs to go home and teach the young; the ambitious have great aims and need shaping. Qian mainly takes 不知所以裁之 as the disciples not knowing how to shape themselves, and does not read 成章 as having written private books.

5.22.title: Bo Yi and Shu Qi were so aloof — why did no one resent them?
5.22.yw: The Master said: Bo Yi and Shu Qi did not keep old wrongs in mind, and so resentment was rare.
5.22.常见读法: Bo Yi and Shu Qi were so high-minded and aloof — why did no one resent them?
5.22.字眼: “怨是用希” — “shi yong” means therefore, “xi” means few; “浼” is read měi, to soil; in “所恶” the “恶” is read wù.
5.22.诸家: Zhu Xi cites Mencius: “不立于恶人之朝，不与恶人言……望望然去之，若将浼焉。其介如此，宜若无所容矣” — they would not stand at a bad man's court nor speak with a bad man, and left in haste as if he would soil them; so fastidious, you would think no one could live with them; “然其所恶之人，能改即止，故人亦不甚怨之也” — yet once those they disliked mended their ways they stopped, so people did not much resent them. He cites Master Cheng: “不念旧恶，此清者之量” — not keeping old wrongs in mind is the magnanimity of the pure; “二子之心，非夫子孰能知之” — who but the Master could know the hearts of these two?
5.22.片里落点: So fastidious they seemed to tolerate no one, yet they stopped once a person changed, so few resented them; the measure of the pure is not keeping old accounts. Today: the neighbour you once quarrelled with apologised, and you still nod to each other on the stairs.

zb_say.qian: Qian: Bo Yi and Shu Qi themselves held no resentment, their hearts unclogged; Zhu: others rarely resented them because they did not hold old wrongs in mind.

5.23.title: Why is borrowing something for a neighbour not upright?
5.23.yw: The Master said: Who says Weisheng Gao is upright? Someone asked him for vinegar; he begged it from his neighbour and gave it to them.
5.23.常见读法: He borrowed something on another's behalf — why would that count as not upright?
5.23.字眼: “醯” is read xī, vinegar; “乞” is read qǐ; “徇” is read xùn; in “掠美” the “掠” is read lüè.
5.23.诸家: Zhu Xi: “微生姓，高名，鲁人，素有直名者” — surname Weisheng, given name Gao, a man of Lu long reputed upright; “夫子言此，讥其曲意徇物，掠美市恩，不得为直也” — the Master says this to mock him for bending his intent to please others, taking credit and buying goodwill, which cannot be called upright. He cites Master Cheng: “微生高所枉虽小，害直为大” — the bend was small, but the harm to uprightness is great; and Fan: “是曰是，非曰非，有谓有，无谓无，曰直。圣人观人于其一介之取予，而千驷万钟从可知焉” — yes for yes, no for no, have for have, have-not for have-not: that is upright; the sage judges a man by the smallest taking and giving, and from that one knows how he would handle a thousand teams of horses.
5.23.片里落点: Saying “I don't have any” is upright; passing off a borrowed thing as your own is bending to please — a small matter, but Master Cheng says what it harms is uprightness itself. Today: a colleague asks for a charging cable, you borrow one from the next desk and say “Here, use mine.”

zb_say.qian: Both: having no vinegar, he did not say so straight but begged it from a neighbour to give, bending to please and buying goodwill, so he cannot be called upright; both judge a person from small things, not the vinegar itself as evil.

5.24.title: Why did Confucius find excessive politeness shameful?
5.24.yw: The Master said: Fine words, an ingratiating face, excessive deference — Zuoqiu Ming was ashamed of them, and I too am ashamed of them. Hiding resentment and befriending the man — Zuoqiu Ming was ashamed of it, and I too am ashamed of it.
5.24.常见读法: Being too polite is surely harmless — why did Confucius find it shameful?
5.24.字眼: In “足恭”, “足” is read jù; Zhu Xi: “将树反。足，过也” — pronounced jù; it means excessive; “匿” is read nì; “窬” is read yú (“穿窬”, thieves who dig through or climb over walls).
5.24.诸家: Zhu Xi cites Master Cheng: “左丘明，古之闻人也” — Zuoqiu Ming was a renowned man of old; and Xie: “二者之可耻，有甚于穿窬也。左丘明耻之，其所养可知矣。夫子自言丘亦耻之，盖窃比老彭之意。又以深戒学者，使察乎此而立心以直也” — these two are more shameful than burglary; that Zuoqiu Ming was ashamed of them shows his cultivation; the Master's “I too am ashamed” carries the sense of modestly comparing himself to Lao Peng, and deeply warns learners to examine this and set their hearts on uprightness.
5.24.片里落点: Both shames are a gap between inside and outside: sweet words, smiles and excessive courtesy to curry favour; befriending someone while nursing a grudge is pretence. Xie says it is worse than theft, because the heart is not upright. Today: holding a grudge, yet being the first at the table to raise a glass to him.

zb_say.qian: Qian takes 足恭 as making a show of reverence with one's feet, paired with clever words and an ingratiating face; Zhu reads 足 as excess: excessive reverence. Both are ashamed of hiding resentment and befriending the person.

5.25.title: Why was Confucius' wish greater than Zilu's and Yan Yuan's?
5.25.yw: Yan Yuan and Ji Lu were attending. The Master said: Why not each tell me your wishes? Zilu said: I would like to share my carriage, horses, clothes and light furs with my friends, and feel no regret if they wear them out. Yan Yuan said: I would like not to boast of my good points, nor make a show of my merits. Zilu said: We would like to hear your wishes, Master. The Master said: That the old be at ease, friends have trust, and the young be cherished.
