5.25.常见读法: Why is Confucius' wish greater than those of Zilu and Yan Yuan?
5.25.字眼: “盍” — why not; “衣” is read in the departing tone, to wear; “敝” — worn out; “伐” — to boast; “施” — to make a show of. Zhu Xi gives two readings of “劳”: merit (as in “劳而不伐”) or toilsome tasks (not wishing to impose them on others), and says “亦通” — either works.
5.25.诸家: Zhu Xi: “老者养之以安，朋友与之以信，少者怀之以恩” — care for the old so they are at ease, deal with friends in good faith, cherish the young with kindness; another reading, “安之，安我也；信之，信我也；怀之，怀我也。亦通” — the old are at ease with me, friends trust me, the young turn to me, also works. He cites Master Cheng: “夫子安仁，颜渊不违仁，子路求仁” — the Master rests in ren, Yan Yuan does not depart from ren, Zilu seeks ren; “子路、颜渊、孔子之志，皆与物共者也，但有小大之差尔” — all three wishes are about sharing with others, differing only in scale; and “羁靮以御马而不以制牛……须要识得圣贤气象” — bridles are for horses, not oxen... one must learn to recognise the bearing of sages and worthies.
5.25.片里落点: All three share with others, differing in scale: Zilu shares carriage and horses with friends, Yan Yuan does not boast or show off, Confucius lets each find their place, like heaven and earth nurturing without a trace. Today: the auntie in the housing block whom the elderly trust with their keys and to whose door the children run first after school.

zb_say.qian: Qian joins 共敝之 and drops the word 轻; Zhu breaks the sentence at 共. 伐善 and 施劳 are glossed alike; for 老安、友信、少怀 Zhu keeps both directions of reading.

5.26.title: Why is it so hard to see one's own faults?
5.26.yw: The Master said: It is hopeless! I have yet to see anyone who can see his own faults and bring the charge against himself inwardly.
5.26.常见读法: Why is it so hard to see one's own mistakes?
5.26.字眼: “讼” originally means to dispute (Shuowen: “讼，争也”); “内自讼” is holding a trial against oneself in one's heart; “咎” is read jiù; “鲜” is read xiǎn, few.
5.26.诸家: Zhu Xi: “已矣乎者，恐其终不得见而叹之也。内自讼者，口不言而心自咎也” — “it is hopeless” is a sigh for fear he will never see such a person; “bringing the charge inwardly” means saying nothing aloud but blaming oneself in the heart; “人有过而能自知者鲜矣，知过而能内自讼者为尤鲜。能内自讼，则其悔悟深切而能改必矣。夫子自恐终不得见而叹之，其警学者深矣” — few people with faults know them; fewer still, knowing them, can arraign themselves inwardly; one who can will repent deeply and surely change; the Master sighs for fear of never seeing it, a deep warning to learners. Zhu Xi cites no other commentator here.
5.26.片里落点: Two levels: knowing one's fault is already rare; knowing it and blaming oneself inwardly is rarer still; only self-arraignment leads to thorough change. Confucius' sigh of “never seen” is a warning to learners. Today: she misreported a figure in a meeting and nobody noticed, and after the meeting she messaged everyone to correct it.

zb_say.qian: Both: 已矣乎 sighs for fear of never seeing it; 内自讼 is seeing one's fault and blaming oneself within, not mere verbal admission. Qian further links it to Yan Hui not repeating faults.

5.27.title: The one thing Confucius claimed to have more of
5.27.yw: The Master said: In a hamlet of ten households there are surely people as loyal and trustworthy as I am, but none as fond of learning as I am.
5.27.常见读法: Is the only thing Confucius claimed to have more of than others just one thing?
5.27.字眼: “焉” is read yān; Zhu Xi: “如字，属上句” — read normally, belonging to the preceding clause (break after “如丘者焉”); the “好” of “好学” is in the departing tone; “邑” — a small settlement; “质” — native endowment.
5.27.诸家: Zhu Xi: “十室，小邑也。忠信如圣人，生质之美者也” — ten households is a small settlement; loyalty and trustworthiness like a sage's are a fine native endowment; “夫子生知而未尝不好学，故言此以勉人。言美质易得，至道难闻，学之至则可以为圣人，不学则不免为乡人而已。可不勉哉” — the Master knew by birth yet never ceased to love learning, so he said this to encourage others: fine endowments are easy to find, the highest Way is hard to hear; learning to the utmost one can become a sage, without learning one remains a villager. How can one not strive?
5.27.片里落点: Loyalty and trust are the base, found everywhere; love of learning is effort, and rare. Confucius does not boast of innate knowledge, only of loving to learn, to encourage others. The Gongye Chang book ends here. Today: honest, reliable people are everywhere; people still going to night school at sixty are few.

zb_say.qian: Both: even a small settlement has the native gift of loyalty and good faith, but loving learning to perfect virtue is rare; one must not rely on gifts and skip learning. Qian further rejects making the sage purely born knowing rather than learned; the Zhu and Zhang quoted by Zhu also stress learning.

6.1.title: Why can one's affairs be simple but not one's heart?
6.1.yw: The Master said: Yong could be given the seat facing south. Zhonggong asked about Zisang Bozi. The Master said: He will do; he is simple. Zhonggong said: To dwell in reverence and act simply in governing the people — is that not acceptable? But to dwell in simplicity and act simply — is that not too simple? The Master said: Yong's words are right.
6.1.常见读法: Why can affairs be handled simply, but the heart must not be simple?
6.1.字眼: “南面者，人君听治之位” — facing south is the ruler's seat for hearing government; “可者，仅可而有所未尽之辞。简者，不烦之谓” — “will do” means barely acceptable, with something lacking; “simple” means not fussy; the “大” of “大简” is read tài; the “衣” of “不衣冠而处” is in the departing tone, to wear. Zisang Bozi, Hu suspects, is the Zisang Hu mentioned in Zhuangzi.
6.1.诸家: Zhu Xi: “言自处以敬，则中有主而自治严……岂不失之大简，而无法度之可守乎” — if one holds oneself in reverence, there is a master within and self-discipline is strict … otherwise is it not too simple, with no rules to keep? He cites the Kongzi Jiayu: Bozi “不衣冠而处，夫子讥其欲同人道于牛马” — lived without proper clothes and cap; the Master mocked him for wanting to make human ways like those of oxen and horses; and Master Cheng: “居敬则心中无物，故所行自简；居简则先有心于简，而多一简字矣，故曰大简” — dwelling in reverence, the heart holds nothing extra, so action is naturally simple; dwelling in simplicity, one first sets one's mind on simplicity, adding one more “simple”, hence “too simple”.
6.1.片里落点: With a settled heart and respect in everything, affairs become simple of themselves; aiming first at ease and letting yourself off too is too simple. Today: in the team with the fewest rules, the person in charge is the most punctual and best organised of all.

zb_say.yang: Yang 6.1, 南面: Yang takes it broadly as the seat of any chief, from the Son of Heaven and lords to ministers and grandees; Zhu specifically as the ruler's seat for hearing government, showing Zhonggong had a ruler's capacity; the scope differs. Yang 6.2, 简: Yang explicitly adopts Zhu's “affairs not troublesome, the people not disturbed”; Yang does not adopt identifications of Zisang Bozi such as Zisang Hu, and Zhu records Hu's guess that he was Zisang Hu without proof.
zb_say.qian: Both: 南面 is the ruler's seat, 可 is barely acceptable, 简 is not troublesome; both separate dwelling in reverence and acting simply from dwelling in simplicity and acting simply, approving strict self-discipline that does not trouble the people.

6.2.title: Why is Confucius' “love of learning” not about reading a lot?
6.2.yw: Duke Ai asked: Which of your disciples loves learning? Confucius replied: There was Yan Hui who loved learning. He did not shift his anger, and did not repeat a fault. Unfortunately his life was short and he died. Now there is none; I have not heard of anyone who loves learning.
6.2.常见读法: Why does Confucius' “love of learning” not mean reading a lot?
6.2.字眼: “好” in the departing tone; “亡，与无同” — “wang” is the same as “none”; “迁，移也。贰，复也” — “qian” is to move, “er” is to repeat; Yan Hui “三十二而卒” — died at thirty-two (as Zhu Xi records).
6.2.诸家: Master Cheng: “颜子之怒，在物不在己，故不迁。有不善未尝不知，知之未尝复行，不贰过也” — Yanzi's anger lay in the thing, not in himself, so it did not shift; whenever there was something not good he always knew it, and having known it never did it again: that is not repeating a fault; “喜怒在事，则理之当喜怒者也，不在血气则不迁” — when joy and anger lie in the matter, they are what principle calls for; not lying in the blood and breath, they do not shift; “如鉴之照物，妍媸在彼，随物应之而已” — like a mirror reflecting things, beauty and ugliness are in them; it simply responds to each. Master Zhang: “慊于己者，不使萌于再” — what dissatisfies oneself is not allowed to sprout a second time. Master Cheng on learning: “学以至乎圣人之道” — learning is to reach the Way of the sage; “约其情使合于中，正其心，养其性” — restrain the feelings to accord with the mean, rectify the heart, nourish the nature; and he ends mocking “今人乃谓圣本生知，非学可至，而所以为学者，不过记诵文辞之间，其亦异乎颜子之学矣” — people now say sagehood is innate and cannot be reached by learning, and their learning is nothing but memorising and composing — far from Yanzi's learning.
6.2.片里落点: Love of learning lies in governing one's feelings: not shifting anger onto others, not making the same mistake twice. Today: scolded at work, you still come home, crouch down, and tie your child's shoelaces properly.

zb_say.qian: Both: 不迁怒 is anger at A not shifting to B; 不贰过 is not repeating a fault. Qian stresses faults already shown in conduct and does not mainly reduce Yan Hui's faults to tiny unformed stirrings of thought; Zhu also cites that layer.

6.3.title: Why did Confucius give one man little grain and another a lot?
6.3.yw: Zihua was sent on a mission to Qi, and Ranzi asked for grain for his mother. The Master said: Give her a fu. He asked for more. The Master said: Give her a yu. Ranzi gave her five bing of grain. The Master said: When Chi went to Qi he rode fat horses and wore light furs. I have heard that the gentleman helps the needy, not adds to the rich. When Yuan Si became his steward, he was given nine hundred measures of grain, and declined. The Master said: Don't! Give it to your neighbours and villagers.
6.3.常见读法: Both were gifts of grain — why did Confucius give one little and the other a lot?
6.3.字眼: “使、为，并去声” — “shi” and “wei” are both in the departing tone; a fu is six dou four sheng, a yu sixteen dou, a bing sixteen hu; “衣” in the departing tone, to wear; “急，穷迫也。周者，补不足。继者，续有余” — “ji” is dire need; “zhou” is making up a lack; “ji” (continue) is adding to a surplus; “毋，禁止辞” — “wu” is a word of prohibition.
6.3.诸家: Master Cheng: “圣人宽容，不欲直拒人，故与之少，所以示不当与也……求未达而自与之多，则已过矣” — the sage is tolerant and does not wish to refuse flatly, so he gave little to show it should not be given … Qiu did not understand and gave a lot on his own, which was going too far; “原思为宰，则有常禄。思辞其多，故又教以分诸邻里之贫者，盖亦莫非义也” — as steward Yuan Si had a regular salary; when he declined it as too much, the Master taught him to share it with the poor of his neighbourhood: this too was right. Master Zhang: “于斯二者，可见圣人之用财矣” — in these two cases one sees how the sage uses wealth.
6.3.片里落点: How much to give depends not on favour but on what is right. Zihua's family rode fat horses and wore light furs, not in need, so he gave only a little, refusing to add to the rich; Yuan Si's salary was owed by his post, and refusing it would be wrong, so any excess should go to his neighbours. One case is “help the needy, not the rich”; the other is “a regular salary should not be declined”.

zb_say.qian: Same reading of helping the needy, not adding to the rich, and that a regular salary may be shared with neighbours; the 庾 measure differs: Qian takes two dou four sheng added on top of the 釜, Zhu sixteen dou.

6.4.title: Can someone of bad background be employed?
6.4.yw: The Master, speaking of Zhonggong, said: If the calf of a brindled ox is red and well-horned, even if people would rather not use it, would the spirits of the hills and rivers reject it?
6.4.常见读法: Can a person of poor background be employed?
6.4.字眼: “犁，利之反” — “li” is read lí, brindled; “骍，息营反” — “xing” is read xīng, red; “舍，上声” — “she” in the rising tone; “言人虽不用，神必不舍也” — though people may not use it, the spirits will surely not reject it.
6.4.诸家: Zhu Xi: “仲弓父贱而行恶，故夫子以此譬之……然此论仲弓云尔，非与仲弓言也” — Zhonggong's father was lowly and behaved badly, so the Master used this comparison … but this is speaking about Zhonggong, not speaking to him. Fan: “以瞽瞍为父而有舜，以鲧为父而有禹……子能改父之过，变恶以为美，则可谓孝矣” — with Gusou as father there was Shun, with Gun as father there was Yu … a son who can correct his father's faults and turn bad into good may be called filial.
6.4.片里落点: A calf of a brindled plough-ox, pure red with well-formed horns: even if people will not sacrifice it because of its origin, the spirits of hills and rivers will not reject it. A father's badness cannot cancel a son's goodness; Zhu Xi notes specifically that this speaks about Zhonggong, not to his face.

zb_say.qian: Qian takes it as a plough ox, Zhu as an ox of mixed colouring; both hold a son's goodness should not be discarded for a father's badness. Qian discusses whether it was said to Zhonggong's face and leans to it being a remark about him; Zhu says plainly it was not said to his face.

6.5.title: Where did Yan Hui differ from the others?
6.5.yw: The Master said: As for Hui, his heart could go three months without departing from humaneness; the rest reach it only for a day or a month, and that is all.
6.5.常见读法: Yan Hui and the others: where exactly is the difference?
6.5.字眼: “三月，言其久” — “three months” means a long time; “日月至焉，或日一至焉，或月一至焉，能造其域而不能久也” — “reach it for a day or a month” means arriving once a day or once a month: they can enter the domain but cannot stay long.
6.5.诸家: Master Cheng: “三月，天道小变之节，言其久也……过此则圣人矣” — three months is a minor turn in the course of heaven, meaning a long time … beyond this one would be a sage. Yin: “此颜子于圣人，未达一间者也” — here Yanzi falls short of the sage by a hair. Master Zhang: “始学之要，当知三月不违与日月至焉内外宾主之辨” — the key for a beginner is to know the distinction of inside and outside, host and guest, between “three months without departing” and “reaching it for a day or a month”.
6.5.片里落点: Yan Hui's humaneness is like a host living at home who now and then steps out; the others' is like a guest who drops by now and then. The difference lies in how long it lasts, not in whether it is there.

zb_say.qian: Both: three months means long; Yan Hui could dwell in ren without departing, the others reached it now and then but could not stay. Qian uses the image of host and guest inside and outside a house; Zhu explains by having virtue without selfish desire.

6.6.title: Is a single quality enough to take office?
6.6.yw: Ji Kangzi asked: Can Zhong You be put in charge of government? The Master said: Yóu is decisive; what difficulty would he have in government? He asked: Can Ci be put in charge of government? The Master said: Ci is perceptive; what difficulty would he have in government? He asked: Can Qiu be put in charge of government? The Master said: Qiu is accomplished; what difficulty would he have in government?
6.6.常见读法: Can one quality alone qualify someone for office?
6.6.字眼: “从政，谓为大夫” — “to take part in government” means serving as a grandee; “果，有决断。达，通事理。艺，多才能” — “guo” is decisiveness; “da” is understanding how things work; “yi” is having many skills.
6.6.诸家: Master Cheng: “季康子问三子之才可以从政乎？夫子答以各有所长。非惟三子，人各有所长，能取其长，皆可用也” — Ji Kangzi asked whether the talents of the three could serve in government; the Master answered that each had his strength. Not only these three: everyone has a strength, and if one can take it, all can be employed.
6.6.片里落点: Zilu is decisive, Zigong perceptive, Ran Qiu many-skilled: each has one strength and so can be employed. Using people means taking what they are good at.

zb_say.qian: Both: 从政 is serving as a grandee; 果 is decisiveness, 达 understanding affairs, 艺 many skills; people are employed by their strengths, not implying the three were alike in talent and virtue.

6.7.title: Offered an office, why would he flee?
6.7.yw: The Ji family wanted to make Min Ziqian steward of Bi. Min Ziqian said: Decline it for me tactfully. If anyone comes for me again, I shall surely be on the far side of the Wen.
6.7.常见读法: Invited to take office, why did he say he would run away?
6.7.字眼: “费，音祕” — “费” is read bì; “汶，水名，在齐南鲁北竟上” — the Wen is a river on the border, south of Qi and north of Lu; “闵子不欲臣季氏，令使者善为己辞；言若再来召我，则当去之齐” — Minzi did not wish to serve the Ji family, so he asked the messenger to decline well on his behalf, saying that if they summoned him again he would leave for Qi.
6.7.诸家: Master Cheng: “仲尼之门，能不仕大夫之家者，闵子、曾子数人而已” — in Confucius's school, those able not to serve in a grandee's house were only Minzi, Zengzi and a few others. Xie: “学者能少知内外之分，皆可以乐道而忘人之势……刚则必取祸，柔则必取辱” — if a learner knows a little the difference between inner and outer, he can delight in the Way and forget others' power … too hard and he will surely bring disaster, too soft and he will surely bring disgrace; “然则闵子其贤乎” — so was Minzi not worthy?
6.7.片里落点: He would not become the Ji family's retainer, yet he asked the messenger to decline kindly for him, and if they came again he would cross the river to Qi. Neither defying them head-on nor giving in: too hard invites disaster, too soft invites disgrace.

zb_say.qian: Both: Minzi declined to be steward of Bi because he did not wish to serve the Ji; if called again he would go north to Qi. The Wen river was the border, south of Qi and north of Lu; “on the Wen” means crossing north out of Lu.

6.8.title: Why did Confucius hold his dying student's hand through the window?
6.8.yw: Boniu was ill. The Master went to ask after him, and holding his hand through the window, said: We are losing him; it is fate! That such a man should have such an illness! That such a man should have such an illness!
6.8.常见读法: His student was gravely ill: why did Confucius only hold his hand from outside the window?
6.8.字眼: “夫，音扶” — “夫” is read fú; “有疾，先儒以为癞也” — earlier scholars took the illness to be leprosy; “礼：病者居北牖下，君视之，则迁于南牖下，使君得以南面视己。时伯牛家以此礼尊孔子，孔子不敢当，故不入其室，而自牖执其手，盖与之永诀也” — by ritual the sick lie under the north window; when the ruler visits, they are moved under the south window so the ruler may face south to see them. Boniu's family honoured Confucius with this rite; he did not dare accept it, so he did not enter the room but held his hand through the window, a final farewell; “命，谓天命” — “ming” means heaven's decree.
6.8.诸家: Hou: “伯牛以德行称，亚于颜、闵。故其将死也，孔子尤痛惜之” — Boniu was known for virtuous conduct, second only to Yan and Min; so when he was about to die, Confucius grieved for him especially.
6.8.片里落点: Boniu's family moved the sickbed under the south window, as for a ruler's visit; Confucius did not dare accept that honour, so he did not enter and held his hand through the window in farewell. “That such a man should have such an illness” is said twice: grief that such a person should suffer such a disease, laid at the door of fate.

zb_say.qian: The reason for asking through the window differs: Qian explains by the earthen bed under the south window in Qi and Lu, needing no rite of a ruler visiting a minister; Zhu says the family honoured Confucius as a ruler, he dared not accept, so did not enter.

6.9.title: So poor, what was Yan Hui happy about?
6.9.yw: The Master said: How worthy Hui is! A bamboo basket of rice, a gourd of water, living in a mean alley: others could not bear the hardship, yet Hui does not let it change his joy. How worthy Hui is!
6.9.常见读法: Yan Hui was this poor: what was he happy about?
6.9.字眼: “箪，竹器。食，饭也。瓢，瓠也” — “dan” is a bamboo vessel; “si” is cooked rice; “piao” is a gourd; “颜子之贫如此，而处之泰然，不以害其乐” — Yanzi was this poor, yet bore it calmly and did not let it harm his joy; note the word “其” (his).
6.9.诸家: Master Cheng: “颜子之乐，非乐箪瓢陋巷也，不以贫窭累其心而改其所乐也，故夫子称其贤” — Yanzi's joy was not joy in the basket, gourd and alley; he did not let poverty burden his heart and change what he delighted in, so the Master called him worthy; “其字当玩味，自有深意” — the word “其” deserves pondering; it holds a deep meaning. Zhu Xi's note: “程子之言，引而不发，盖欲学者深思而自得之。今亦不敢妄为之说” — Master Cheng drew the bow without releasing, wishing learners to think deeply and find it themselves; I too dare not explain it rashly.
6.9.片里落点: What he enjoyed was not poverty, but a joy that poverty could not change. Zhu Xi would rather not spell it out, leaving readers to find for themselves what lies in the word “其”.

zb_say.qian: Both: poverty could not change what Yan Hui already delighted in; the basket, gourd and alley themselves are not the source of joy. Qian finds deep meaning in the Song scholars' teaching to seek where Confucius and Yan found joy; Zhu also cites Cheng's words.

6.10.title: He said he lacked the strength: why didn't Confucius believe him?
6.10.yw: Ran Qiu said: It is not that I do not delight in your Way, Master; my strength is not enough. The Master said: Those whose strength is not enough give out halfway. You are drawing a line.
6.10.常见读法: He said his strength was not enough: why did Confucius not believe him?
6.10.字眼: “力不足者，欲进而不能” — lacking strength means wanting to advance but being unable; “画者，能进而不欲，谓之画者，如画地以自限也” — drawing a line means being able to advance but not wanting to, like drawing a line on the ground to limit oneself; “女” is read rǔ, “you”.
6.10.诸家: Hu: “夫子称颜回不改其乐，冉求闻之，故有是言。然使求说夫子之道，诚如口之说刍豢，则必将尽力以求之……此冉求之所以局于艺也” — the Master praised Yan Hui for not changing his joy; Ran Qiu heard it and so said this. But had Qiu truly delighted in the Master's Way as the mouth delights in fine meat, he would surely have exerted all his strength to pursue it … this is why Ran Qiu stayed confined to skills.
6.10.片里落点: Someone truly lacking strength collapses halfway along the road; Ran Qiu drew a line on the ground before setting out. It is not that he cannot, but that he will not.

zb_say.qian: Both: lacking strength is wanting to advance but being unable; drawing a line is being able but unwilling, limiting oneself. Qian reads 中道而废 as setting it down for now to go on when strength returns; Zhu teaches Ran Qiu more directly by contrasting will and ability.

6.11.title: Both are scholars: where is the difference?
6.11.yw: The Master said to Zixia: Be a scholar of the gentleman's kind, not a scholar of the petty man's kind.
6.11.常见读法: Both are men of learning: where is the difference?
6.11.字眼: “儒，学者之称” — “ru” is a name for a learned man.
6.11.诸家: Master Cheng: “君子儒为己，小人儒为人” — the gentleman scholar learns for himself; the petty scholar learns for others. Xie: “君子小人之分，义与利之间而已……虽有及人之功，而不害其为己” — the division between gentleman and petty man lies only between rightness and profit … though his work may benefit others, it does not stop it being for himself; “子夏文学虽有余，然意其远者大者或昧焉，故夫子语之以此” — Zixia had learning to spare, but perhaps was unclear about what is far-reaching and great, so the Master told him this.
6.11.片里落点: Studying the same books, one who learns to make something of himself is a gentleman scholar; one who learns to be seen and to gain advantage is a petty scholar. Profit is not only money; reputation counts too.

zb_say.qian: Qian takes 儒 as an occupation, those versed in the six arts seeking office, which later became a school; Zhu glosses it as a name for scholars. Both stress aims and character, not that having learning and skills makes one a gentleman.

6.12.title: Not taking shortcuts: is that talent?
6.12.yw: Ziyou was steward of Wucheng. The Master said: Have you found good men there? He said: There is one Tantai Mieming, who never takes a shortcut when walking, and has never come to my rooms except on public business.
6.12.常见读法: Never taking a shortcut: does that count as talent?
6.12.字眼: “武城，鲁下邑” — Wucheng was a lesser town of Lu; “澹台姓，灭明名，字子羽” — Tantai is the surname, Mieming the given name, courtesy name Ziyu; “径，路之小而捷者” — “jing” is a small, quick path; “公事，如饮射读法之类” — public business means things like the drinking and archery ceremonies and the reading of the laws.
6.12.诸家: Yang: “为政以人才为先，故孔子以得人为问……非公事不见邑宰，则其有以自守，而无枉己徇人之私可见矣” — in governing, talent comes first, so Confucius asked whether he had found men … not seeing the town steward except on public business shows he could hold to himself, without bending himself to please others. Zhu Xi's note: “持身以灭明为法，则无苟贱之羞；取人以子游为法，则无邪媚之惑” — take Mieming as the model for conducting oneself and one avoids the shame of baseness; take Ziyou as the model for choosing people and one is not misled by flattery.
6.12.片里落点: He never cut through by-paths and never came to the official's door without public business. Someone who holds firm in small things can be relied on in large ones; Ziyou saw that too when judging people.

zb_say.qian: Both: Tantai Mieming took no shortcuts and went to the steward's house only on public business, showing upright self-possession; Confucius asking whether he had found men shows he valued talent, not just results.

6.13.title: He covered the retreat: why wouldn't he admit it?
6.13.yw: The Master said: Meng Zhifan does not boast. When the army fled, he guarded the rear. As they were about to enter the gate, he whipped his horse and said: It is not that I dared to stay behind; my horse would not go forward.
6.13.常见读法: He was the one who covered the retreat: why wouldn't he own it?
6.13.字眼: “殿，去声” — “dian” in the departing tone; “伐，夸功也” — “fa” is boasting of merit; “奔，败走也。军后曰殿” — “ben” is fleeing in defeat; the rear of an army is called “dian”; “策，鞭也” — “ce” is a whip; Hu dates the event to the battle between Qi and Lu in the eleventh year of Duke Ai.
6.13.诸家: Xie: “人能操无欲上人之心，则人欲日消，天理日明，而凡可以矜己夸人者，皆无足道矣……若孟之反，可以为法矣” — if one can keep a heart with no wish to rise above others, selfish desire wanes daily and heavenly principle grows clearer daily, and everything one might pride oneself on before others becomes not worth mentioning … one like Meng Zhifan can be taken as a model.
6.13.片里落点: Holding the rear against the enemy in a rout is great merit, yet as they neared the city gate he whipped his horse and said, “It wasn't that I dared to stay behind; the horse wouldn't go.” Passing the credit to his horse shows a heart with no wish to rise above others.

zb_say.qian: Both: Meng Zhifan covered the rear in defeat and did not boast; whipping his horse at the gate and saying it would not go was a pretext to hide his merit. Not boasting is the chapter's point.

6.14.title: Without a glib tongue or good looks, can one escape trouble?
6.14.yw: The Master said: Without the glibness of the priest Tuo, but with the beauty of Song Zhao, it is hard to escape harm in today's world!
6.14.常见读法: Without eloquence or good looks, is trouble unavoidable?
6.14.字眼: “鮀，徒何反” — “鮀” is read tuó; “祝，宗庙之官。鮀，卫大夫，字子鱼，有口才。朝，宋公子，有美色” — “zhu” is an officer of the ancestral temple; Tuo was a grandee of Wey, courtesy name Ziyu, a skilled talker; Zhao was a prince of Song, handsome; “言衰世好谀悦色，非此难免，盖伤之也” — it says a declining age loves flattery and good looks, and without these one can hardly escape: he was lamenting it.
6.14.片里落点: This is not advice to cultivate eloquence and looks; it is a lament for the times: when the world values only a sweet tongue and a pretty face, honest people can hardly escape harm.

zb_say.qian: The sentence is read differently: Qian: without Tuo's eloquence, having only Zhao's good looks, one can hardly escape harm; Zhu: a declining age loves flattery and good looks, and without these two one can hardly escape. Qian argues against the old reading that good looks instead invite harm.

6.15.title: Everyone goes out by the door: why not by the right way?
6.15.yw: The Master said: Who can go out without using the door? Why then does no one follow this Way?
6.15.常见读法: Everyone leaves by the door: why will people not walk the right road in life?
6.15.字眼: “言人不能出不由户，何故乃不由此道邪？怪而叹之之辞” — no one can go out except by the door, so why do people not follow this Way? Words of wonder and lament.
6.15.诸家: Hong: “人知出必由户，而不知行必由道。非道远人，人自远尔” — people know that going out must be by the door, but not that conduct must follow the Way. It is not that the Way is far from people; people distance themselves from it.
6.15.片里落点: Everyone knows to leave by the door rather than climb the wall; the right road in life lies right in front of us, yet people will not take it. It is not that the Way is far from them; they have wandered away themselves.

zb_say.qian: Both take 何莫 as “why not follow this Way”, a cry of wonder and lament. Qian lists the reading that people use the Way daily without knowing it but does not follow it; Zhu directly takes it as urging people to follow the Way.

6.16.title: Too rough or too polished: which would Confucius prefer?
6.16.yw: The Master said: When substance outweighs refinement, one is rustic; when refinement outweighs substance, one is a clerk. Only when refinement and substance are well blended is one a gentleman.
6.16.常见读法: Too rough or too showy: which would Confucius rather have?
6.16.字眼: “野，野人，言鄙略也。史，掌文书，多闻习事，而诚或不足也。彬彬，犹班班，物相杂而适均之貌” — “ye” is a rustic, coarse and careless; “shi” is a scribe who keeps documents, well-informed and practised but perhaps lacking sincerity; “binbin” is like “banban”, things mixed in just proportion; “学者当损有余，补不足，至于成德，则不期然而然矣” — the learner should reduce the excess and make up the lack; on reaching complete virtue it comes about without being sought.
6.16.诸家: Yang: “文质不可以相胜。然质之胜文，犹之甘可以受和，白可以受采也。文胜而至于灭质，则其本亡矣。虽有文，将安施乎？然则与其史也，宁野” — refinement and substance must not overpower each other. Yet substance exceeding refinement is like sweetness that can take seasoning, or white that can take colour. When refinement prevails to the point of destroying substance, the root is lost; though there is refinement, where would it be applied? So rather than the clerk, better the rustic.
6.16.片里落点: Too much plainness is crude, too much ornament is hollow; only the two in balance make a gentleman. If one must lean, better lean plain: with the base intact, refinement can be added; with the base gone, refinement has nowhere to go.

zb_say.qian: Both: substance over refinement is coarse, refinement over substance is clerkly, the two blended in balance make the gentleman. Qian also mentions temple invocators and scribes; Zhu stresses those keeping documents, practised but lacking sincerity.

6.17.title: Don't crooked people live perfectly well too?
6.17.yw: The Master said: Man lives by uprightness; the crooked live only by luck, having escaped.
6.17.常见读法: People who are not upright still seem to live just fine, don't they?
6.17.诸家: Master Cheng: “生理本直。罔，不直也，而亦生者，幸而免尔” — the principle of life is upright by nature. “Wang” means not upright; that such people also live is only because they have luckily escaped.
6.17.片里落点: People are meant to live upright; the crooked are alive too, not because they deserve it but because they have got away with it by luck.

zb_say.qian: Both: 罔 is not upright, and their living is luck escaping harm. Qian explains that society lives by uprightness, so the crooked live on others' uprightness; Zhu cites Cheng: the principle of life is upright.

6.18.title: Knowing, liking, delighting: what's the difference?
6.18.yw: The Master said: Those who know it are not equal to those who love it; those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
6.18.常见读法: Knowing, loving, delighting: where do they differ?
6.18.字眼: “好” in the departing tone, to love; “乐” is read lè, to delight.
6.18.诸家: Yin: “知之者，知有此道也。好之者，好而未得也。乐之者，有所得而乐之也” — to know it is to know that this Way exists; to love it is to love it without yet having gained it; to delight in it is to have gained something and rejoice in it. Zhang Jingfu: “譬之五谷，知者知其可食者也，好者食而嗜之者也，乐者嗜之而饱者也……此古之学者，所以自强而不息者欤” — compare the five grains: the knower knows they are edible, the lover eats and relishes them, the delighter relishes them and is full … is this not why learners of old strove without ceasing?
6.18.片里落点: Knowing there is this bowl of rice, loving to eat it, and having eaten your fill and being at ease: three levels. The difference is not how much you know, but whether you have actually gained it.

zb_say.qian: Both: three levels, knowing the Way, loving it without yet gaining it, delighting after gaining it, compared to knowing grain is edible, eating and relishing it, being full. Both stress learning the Way until one is inseparable from it.

6.19.title: Was Confucius looking down on people?
6.19.yw: The Master said: To those above the middling, one can speak of higher things; to those below the middling, one cannot speak of higher things.
6.19.常见读法: Is Confucius looking down on people here?
6.19.字眼: “语，告也” — “yu” means to tell; “言教人者，当随其高下而告语之，则其言易入而无躐等之弊也” — one who teaches should speak according to the learner's level; then the words go in easily and there is no fault of skipping steps; “上” is read shàng.
6.19.诸家: Zhang Jingfu: “圣人之道，精粗虽无二致，但其施教，则必因其材而笃焉……使之切问近思，而渐进于高远也” — the sage's Way is one in its fine and coarse parts, but in teaching he always builds on each person's capacity … making them ask closely and reflect on what is near, and so advance gradually to the high and far.
6.19.片里落点: This is not ranking people, but fitting words to the listener: speak too high and the listener cannot catch it, and harm is done. Teach according to capacity, and climb step by step.

zb_say.qian: Both: teach according to capacity and in order, without skipping steps; speaking of lofty things too early does harm. Qian notes 不可 does not forbid learning the higher Way, only that it cannot be reached at once.

6.20.title: Did Confucius believe in spirits?
6.20.yw: Fan Chi asked about wisdom. The Master said: To devote oneself to what is right for the people, and to revere the spirits while keeping them at a distance, may be called wisdom. He asked about humaneness. The Master said: The humane put the difficulty first and the reward after; this may be called humaneness.
6.20.常见读法: Did Confucius believe in ghosts and spirits?
6.20.字眼: “民，亦人也。获，谓得也” — “min” also means people; “huo” means gain; “专用力于人道之所宜，而不惑于鬼神之不可知，知者之事也。先其事之所难，而后其效之所得，仁者之心也” — to put one's effort wholly into what is fitting in the human way and not be confused by the unknowable spirits is the business of the wise; to put first what is hard in a task and only after think of what it yields is the heart of the humane; “此必因樊迟之失而告之” — this must have been said in view of Fan Chi's failings.
6.20.诸家: Master Cheng: “人多信鬼神，惑也。而不信者又不能敬，能敬能远，可谓知矣” — many people believe in spirits, which is confusion; those who do not believe cannot revere them. To be able both to revere and to keep at a distance may be called wisdom; “先难，克己也。以所难为先，而不计所获，仁也” — putting the difficult first is mastering oneself; to take the hard as first without counting the gain is humaneness. Lü: “当务为急，不求所难知；力行所知，不惮所难为” — put urgency on present duties and do not seek what is hard to know; practise vigorously what you know and do not shrink from what is hard to do.
6.20.片里落点: The question is not belief or disbelief, but revering and keeping at a distance: first do fully what human affairs require, revere the spirits without petitioning them; in action, the hard part first and the gain after, without reckoning the benefit in advance.

zb_say.qian: Both: attending to what is fitting in the human way and not being confused by spirits is wisdom. Qian links 敬 and 远 through 民, the people being the spirits' masters; Zhu stresses not being confused by the unknowable spirits, and both take 先难后获 as not counting results.
